more.definition: that (connecting noun clause); that (introducing the result of the main clause); than (used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese que, from Latin quid (“what”) (usurping as well the roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate with English who.

more.definition: which; that; who (of those mentioned); whose; what thing
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese que, from Latin quid (“what”) (usurping as well the roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate with English who.

more.definition: not; don't; haven't (negates the meaning of the verb or adverb); used in sentences containing a negative pronoun as the object; see double negative; used to emphasise or reinforce (in the case that there is a previous unstressed adverb não, see above) sentences containing a negative pronoun as the subject or already containing não
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese non, from Latin nōn (“no”), from Old Latin noenum, from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”) + *óynos (“one”).

more.definition: no (used to show disagreement or negation); no (used to show agreement with a negative question)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese non, from Latin nōn (“no”), from Old Latin noenum, from Proto-Indo-European *né (“not”) + *óynos (“one”).

more.definition: the (the definite grammatical article that shows that the noun phrase that immediately follows it is definitely identifiable...); sometimes after lhe, especially when referring to a body part, a family member, or a pet.; (precedes a familiar nickname or other term of address)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese o (compare Galician o), from Late Latin lo (compare Spanish lo) with loss of initial l, from earlier *illu, from Latin illum m, illud n, accusative singular forms of ille (“the”, “that”).

more.definition: of (in relation to); of (forms compounds; often untranslated); of; about (on the subject of)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese de, from Latin dē, from Proto-Italic *dē, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₁, from *de + *-h₁. Cognate with Galician de.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese a, from Latin a, form of A, from Etruscan 𐌀 (a), from Ancient Greek Α (A, “alpha”), from Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ, “aleph”), from Egyptian 𓃾.

more.definition: to, introduces the indirect object; to; towards, indicates destination; away, indicates a physical distance
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese a, from Latin ad (“to”) and ab (“from, away, by”).

more.definition: her, it (as a direct object; as an indirect object, see lhe; after prepositions, see ela)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese á, from Vulgar Latin *la (compare Spanish, Catalan, Italian, and French la), from Late Latin illa(m), feminine singular of ille (“the”, “that”).

more.definition: Indicates agreement; that's right; yes; yeah.; Used in hesitant speech; erm; um.
second-person singular personal pronoun, formal or informal in Brazil, formal or semi-formal in Portugal; you; indefinite pronoun; you, one
more.etymology: Syncope of vosmecê, elision of vossemecê, contraction of Old Galician-Portuguese vossa mercee (literally “your mercy”) (today's mercê) from Latin vostram + mercēdem. Compare with Spanish usted (from vuestra merced (literally “your mercy”)) and Catalan vostè.

more.definition: and (connects two clauses indicating that the events occurred together, one after the other or without any special implication); and (connects the last and penultimate elements in a list); what about
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese e, from Latin et.

more.definition: I (first-person singular personal pronoun)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese eu, from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆. Doublet of ego.

more.definition: one
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ũu (“one; a”), from Latin ūnum (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”). Doublet of uno.

more.definition: for (directed at, intended to belong to or to be appropriate for); indicates application of an adjective; to; to; so; in order to (indicates purpose)
more.etymology: From earlier pera, from Old Galician-Portuguese pera, from Latin per (“through”) + ad (“to”).

more.definition: if (introduces a condition that may be (or prove to be) either true or false); if (introduces a condition that is counterfactual or hypothetical); if (introduces a condition that is known to be true)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese se, from Latin sī (“if”).

more.definition: with; against; with; alongside; together with (in the company of); with (as a part or accessory of)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese con, from Latin cum (“with”). Compare Fala, Galician, and Spanish con.

more.definition: for (on behalf of); for (in order to obtain); for (over a period of time)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *próder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese por, from Late Latin pōr, from Latin prō (“for”) (with metathetic shift under the influence of per). Usurped the roles of Latin per.

more.definition: third-person masculine singular nominative personal pronoun; he; it; third-person masculine singular prepositional pronoun; him; it; third-person masculine singular personal pronoun used in all positions; he; him; it
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₂el-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ele, from Latin ille (“that, he, she, it”).

more.definition: that (the thing near you; the thing mentioned that concerns you); this (the thing near me; the thing mentioned that concerns me)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese esso, from Latin ipsum, neuter of ipse (“itself”).

more.definition: in; inside; within (contained by); on; on top of (located just above the surface of); in; at (located in a location)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese en, from Latin in (“in”), from Proto-Italic *en, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”). Doublet of in.

more.definition: emphasises a previous clause, adverb or adjective; really; and how
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mas, from Latin magis (“more”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“great”). Doublet of mais.

more.definition: but (introduces a clause that contradicts the implications of the previous clause); but (introduces the correct information for something that was denied in the previous clause); but ... really; of course; no wonder (introduces the cause of the previous clause, with the implication that the result was expected given this cause)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mas, from Latin magis (“more”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“great”). Doublet of mais.

more.definition: how (in what way, manner); why; how could (for what cause, reason, or purpose), when the action is considered reproachful; such as; like; for example: introduces an example or list of examples
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese como (“how; in what way”), from Latin cōmō̆, a non-literary form of quōmodo.

more.definition: but also; as well as (introduces an exceptional characteristic); like; as (in the same way that; according to what); as; because; since (introduces a reason or motive)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese como (“how; in what way”), from Latin cōmō̆, a non-literary form of quōmodo.

more.definition: well; accurately; competently; well; fairly; rather (to a significant degree); very; really (to a high degree)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ben, from Latin bene (“well”).

more.definition: good (the ensemble of forces that conspire for good, as opposed to evil); good; well-being; a good deed
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ben, from Latin bene (“well”).

more.definition: third-person plural direct objective personal pronoun; them
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese os, from Vulgar Latin *los, from Latin illōs.

more.definition: third-person feminine singular nominative pronoun she; it; third-person feminine singular prepositional pronoun her; third-person feminine singular pronoun used in all positions she; it; her
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ela, from Latin illa, feminine of ille. Cognate with Galician ela and Spanish ella.

more.definition: yes (affirmative answer)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sóder. Portuguese nãoinflu. Portuguese miminflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese si (“yes”), influenced by não or mim.

more.definition: here (in this place); hither (to this place); here (at this time; at the present situation)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese aqui, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hīc, etymologically Latin eccum (“here he is!”) + hīc (“here”).

more.definition: used to form the comparative of adjectives and adverbs; more; -er; preceded by the definitive article, used to form the superlative of adjectives and adverbs; most; -est; more (to a greater degree or extent)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mais, from Latin magis (“more”). Doublet of mas. Displaced collateral form chus.

more.definition: mine (used predicatively); mine (used absolutely, set off from the sentence)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese meu, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.

more.definition: his (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of him); hers (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of her); its
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese seu, sou, from Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé (“self”).

more.definition: very; a lot; very much (to a great extent or degree)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese muito, from Latin multus (“much; many”), from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Aragonese muito, Catalan molt, Galician moito, Italian molto, Romanian mult, Spanish mucho.

more.definition: much; many; a lot of; lots of; too much; too many (an excessive amount of)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese muito, from Latin multus (“much; many”), from the Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Aragonese muito, Catalan molt, Galician moito, Italian molto, Romanian mult, Spanish mucho.

more.definition: forms the analytic first-person plural imperative; let's
everything (all the things); everything that is essential; everyone; all (all people in general or in a specific group)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese todo, from Latin tōtus (“all; everything”).

more.definition: only; just (alone in a category); only; just (no more than); only; merely; just (introduces a number or object with the implication that it is small or insufficient)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese soo, from Latin sōlus (“alone”). Doublet of solo.

more.definition: only; just (indicates that no other action is/was/will be performed); only; merely; just; simply (indicates that the action is not significant); alone (unaccompanied or without help)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese soo, from Latin sōlus (“alone”). Doublet of solo.

more.definition: then (at that time); then (soon afterwards; after that)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese enton, from Vulgar Latin *in tunc, from Latin in + tunc (“then”). Displaced collateral form entonce. Compare Spanish entonces.

more.definition: now; right now (at the present time); now; any more (differently from the past); just now (very recently)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese agora, from Latin hāc hōrā. Compare Galician agora and Spanish ahora. To a lesser extent, compare also Italian ora and Old French ore.

more.definition: to be (to have the given quality), especially a quality that is intrinsic or not expected to change, contrasting with estar which denotes a temporary quality; to be (to be an example or type of, or the same as); to be; forms the passive voice
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ser, from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. The forms sou (“I am”) and sois pl (“you are”) derive from a Vulgar Latin *sonō and *sutis. Along the way, the verb absorbed Old Galician-Portuguese seer < Latin sedēre (“sit”). The latter supplied the present subjunctive of modern ser, where /-ʒ-/ reflects Late Latin /-(d)j-/, as in seja < sedeat).

more.definition: when (used in questions about time); when (during which)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quando, from Latin quandō.

more.definition: when (at such time); when (whilst on the contrary)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quando, from Latin quandō.

senses.gloss_en: to put, to add, to pour
to create, to shape, to make

more.definition: to create; to produce; to do; to execute; to perform; to cause to
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fazer. Compare Galician facer, Spanish hacer, Italian fare.

more.definition: masculine third-person plural nominative personal pronoun; they; masculine third-person plural prepositional pronoun; them; masculine third-person plural personal pronoun used in all positions; they; them
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese elos, from Latin illōs, influenced by the singular form.

more.definition: first-person plural nominative personal pronoun: we; first-person plural prepositional pronoun: us
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nos, from Latin nōs (“we; us”), from Proto-Italic *nōs.

more.definition: right; correct (not containing errors); certain; sure (without doubt); precise; accurate
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese certo, from Latin certus (“certain”), past participle of cernō (“to sift; to discern”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to move; to separate”).

more.definition: correctly; surely
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese certo, from Latin certus (“certain”), past participle of cernō (“to sift; to discern”), from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to move; to separate”).

more.definition: already (indicating that something has happened before); now (at this instant); any more; any longer
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ja, from Latin iam (“already”). Compare Spanish ya.

more.definition: who; whom (which person?); who; whom; that (the person who[m] or that); those who; people who; anyone who; who(m)ever
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese quen, from Latin quem (“whom”), accusative case of interrogative quis (“who?”) and relative quī (“who”).

more.definition: or (connects at least two alternative words, phrases, clauses, sentences, etc. each of which could make a passage true); or (connects two equivalent names); either … or
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ou, from Latin aut.

more.definition: nothing (not any thing; no thing)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese nada, from Latin (nūlla rēs) nāta (literally “no born thing, not a thing born”).

more.definition: there (in that place, far from both the speaker and the audience); used with an adverb phrase to indicate that something is far; used to emphasize a relative distant point in the past or in the future
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ala, from Latin ad (“to”) + illāc (“that way”).

more.definition: where; wherever (in or at what place; in or at a/any/the place that, in what situation); where (the place in or at which)
more.etymology: Latin *cundeder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese onde, from Latin unde (“whence”). Compare Spanish donde.

translations.de: Das Essen hier ist sehr gut.
translations.en: The food here is very good.
translations.fr: La nourriture ici est très bonne.

more.definition: desirable, positive, advantageous; pleasant, enjoyable, (of food) tasty; kind, generous, acting morally
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bõo, inherited from Latin bonus (“good”), from Old Latin duonos, earlier duenos, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Doublet of bónus /bônus, a later borrowing. Compare Fala and Galician bo, Spanish bueno.

senses.gloss_en: to get, to receive, to be given

more.definition: to own; to possess; to have; to have got; to be rich, to have plenty of money; or, to have enough money to live comfortably; to have as a component or to consist of
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese teer, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese tẽer, Latin tenēre.

more.definition: to speak; to pronounce; to utter; to say; to tell; to say (to communicate information to someone); to say (to indicate a given fact)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dizer, from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”). Compare Galician dicir.

more.definition: on; atop; on top of (located on the top surface of); over; above (in or through the space above); about; concerning (on the subject of)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sobre, from Latin super, from *eks-uper, which consists of Proto-Indo-European *eḱs (“out of”) and *uperi. Doublet of the borrowed super. Cognate to Spanish sobre, French sur, Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”) and English over, super and sur-.

more.definition: European Portuguese standard spelling of por que; pre-reform spelling (used until 1943) of por que; now a common misspelling
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porque, from Vulgar Latin [Term?]. By surface analysis, univerbation of por (“for”) + que (“that”). Doublet of por que. Cognate with Galician and Spanish porque, Catalan perquè, French parce que and Italian perché.

more.definition: because (introduces a reason for that described in the previous clause); because (introduces an explanation to a claim in the previous clause)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porque, from Vulgar Latin [Term?]. By surface analysis, univerbation of por (“for”) + que (“that”). Doublet of por que. Cognate with Galician and Spanish porque, Catalan perquè, French parce que and Italian perché.

more.definition: same (not different; not another); same (similar; alike; analogous); used as an intensifier
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mesmo, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese meesmo, from Vulgar Latin of Iberia *medesmo, from proto-Romanic forms as *medessimu, from *medissimu, from *medipsimu, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from a previous *metipsissīmus, derived from Latin -met (emphatic suffix) + ipse (“himself”) + -issimus (superlative suffix). Compare with Spanish mismo, French même.

more.definition: really; actually; in fact; simply, just; even (implying an extreme example in the case mentioned)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mesmo, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese meesmo, from Vulgar Latin of Iberia *medesmo, from proto-Romanic forms as *medessimu, from *medissimu, from *medipsimu, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from a previous *metipsissīmus, derived from Latin -met (emphatic suffix) + ipse (“himself”) + -issimus (superlative suffix). Compare with Spanish mismo, French même.

more.definition: thing (a physical object, entity, or situation); thingamajig; gizmo, thingy (something whose name is unknown)
more.etymology: Alteration of cousa, from Old Galician-Portuguese cousa, from Latin causa (“cause, reason”), meaning "thing" in Late and Vulgar Latin. Doublet of causa, a learned borrowing. Compare Galician cousa, Spanish, Italian, and Catalan cosa, and French chose.

more.definition: something (unspecified object)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese algo, from Latin aliquod (“some; a few”).

more.definition: until (up to the time of something happening); by (at some point before the given time); to (all the way to a place)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese até, ata of uncertain origin. Possibly from Arabic حَتَّى (ḥattā), Latin ad ista (“to this”) or Latin ad tenus (“as far as”) (>"ad tenes"), which explain the large number of mediaeval variants (atrõe, atée, atrõo, attaa, atẽe, atães, tẽe and so on). However, considering the rarity of tenus, possibly from Latin intrā. Compare Spanish hasta, Leonese ata, Asturian ta.

more.definition: time (the progression from the present into the future); time (quantity of availability of duration); a duration of time, especially a long one
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese tempo, from Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).

more.definition: never (at no time; not ever)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nunca, from Latin numquam (“never”).

more.definition: you (second-person plural personal pronoun)
that, that one (near you); that (that one); this (this one) (indicates something already mentioned or understood from context)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esse, from Latin ipse (“himself”).

more.definition: structure serving as an abode of human beings; building or institution serving as something other than residence, such as a shop; noble family
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese casa, from Latin casa (“cottage”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to link or weave together; chain, net; hut, shed”).

more.definition: catafalque (platform to display or convey a coffin)
more.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ersa, past participle of ērigēre (“to erect”).

more.definition: to see; to observe (to perceive with one’s eyes); to see (to be able to see; not to be blind or blinded); to see; to understand
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese veer, from Latin vidēre (“to see”), from Proto-Italic *widēō (“I see”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”).

more.definition: too; also (in addition; as well); not only … but also
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tan ben, from tan (“as, so”) (modern tão) + ben (“well”) (modern bem). Compare with Spanish también and English as well.

more.definition: still, yet (up to a time); even (emphasises a comparative); someday (at some time in the future)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese aynda, from paragogic a- + inda, from Latin inde (“thenceforth”).

more.definition: so (to a great extent); as … as; eye dialect spelling of então
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sóder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tan, from Latin tam (“so”).

more.definition: face; heads (side of coin); resemblance, appearance; look (perceived characteristic of a person, object or situation)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cara, from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara, from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára, “head, face”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrh₂esn.

translations.de: Sie ist gestern ins Kino gegangen.

translations.fr: Elle est allée au cinéma hier.

more.definition: to go (to move to a destination); will; to be going to; forms the future tense; to keep on; to go on; ~ on; forms the continuative aspect
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ir, from Latin īre. The forms beginning with /v/ derive from corresponding forms of Latin vādere; those beginning with /f/ derive from corresponding forms of Latin esse, which are a result of suppletion with ser (“to be”).

usage_note: In spoken Brazilian Portuguese "ir em" is also heard: vou no cinema.

more.definition: night (period between sunset and sunrise); nightlife
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese noite, from Latin noctem, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

more.definition: -less; without (not having, containing, characteristic of, etc.); without (not doing or not having done something); no (indicates lack of possibility or allowance)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sen, from Latin sine, from Proto-Indo-European *sene.

more.definition: thanks; thank you
more.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin obligātus (“obliged”), past participle of obligō (“to bind in obligation”).

more.definition: period between sunrise and sunset; period from midnight to the following midnight; period of 24 hours
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dia, from Vulgar Latin *dia, first-declension reshaping of Classical Latin diēs, reformed from the accusative diem, from Proto-Italic *djēm, the accusative of *djous (“day, sky”), from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Distantly related to Deus, Zeus and Jove.

more.definition: perhaps; maybe (indicates possibility or doubt)
more.etymology: From tal (“such”) + vez (“time”).

more.definition: father (male who sires a child); one's father; parent (either a mother or a father)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pay < *pade, child-speech forms of padre, from Latin patrem, the accusative of pater (“father”), from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr (“father”). Doublet of padre. Compare mãe (“mother”), which underwent a similar phonetic reduction from its root (Latin mater), and, in addition, was nasalized, perhaps because it was more frequently used than this word.

more.definition: god; deity
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese deus (“God”), from Latin deus (“god, deity”), unusual in that it was derived from the nominative instead of the accusative (deum), from Old Latin deivos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Italic *deiwos (“god, deity”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god, deity”), from *dyew- (“sky, heaven”).

more.definition: somebody; someone (some person)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese alguen, conflation of algũ and quen. Compare Spanish alguien, Galician alguén.

more.definition: mother (female who gives birth to or parents a child); one's mother; mother (source or origin)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mãy, nasalization of earlier *mae < *made, child-speech forms of madre, from Latin mātrem, the accusative of māter (“mother”). Doublet of madre. Compare pai (“father”), which underwent a similar phonetic reduction from its root (Latin pater), but was not nasalized. Cognate with Galician mai, nai, Mirandese, Leonese, and Aragonese mai and Asturian ma.

more.definition: state of being alive; lifetime (period during which someone is alive or something exists); living conditions
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *gʷeyh₃-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vida, from Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā.

more.definition: alternative letter-case form of senhor (used before a name); Mister
a man (an adult male human); gentleman (a respectable man); an old man
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese senhor m or f by sense, from Latin senior, seniōrem (“older (one)”, “elder (one)”, used as a title of respect in Medieval Latin), the comparative of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos (“old”). Doublet of sénior /sênior. Compare Occitan senhor, sénher, signour, Spanish and Galician señor.

more.definition: this one (indicates something or someone nearby); this one (indicates something or someone about to be mentioned); this (which is current)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese este (displacing collateral form aqueste), from Latin iste.

more.definition: this (the thing here); this (the thing being discussed; the current situation)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese isto, from Latin istud, neuter of iste (“that”).

more.definition: always (at all times); always (regularly at stated intervals)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sem-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sempre, from Latin semper. Compare Catalan sempre and Spanish siempre.

more.definition: time; occasion; move (chance to use something shared in sequence with others); turn; move (one’s chance to make a move in a game having two or more players)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese vez (displacing vegada), from Latin vicis (“change, alternation”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to wind, bend”).

more.definition: truth (conformity to fact or reality); truth (true facts); a true statement or fact
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese verdade, from Latin vēritātem (“truth”).

senses.gloss_en: to become, to get, to grow

more.definition: to become; to get; to end up; to be, to be located; to stay (at); to remain (in)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ficar (also fincar), from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“drive in, fix in place”). Doublet of fincar.

senses.gloss_en: oh, oh no, you don’t, say

more.definition: light (pale in colour); bright (luminous; not dark); clear (without clouds nor fog)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin clārus (“clear; bright”), displacing Old Galician-Portuguese craro.

more.definition: clearly (without ambiguity)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin clārus (“clear; bright”), displacing Old Galician-Portuguese craro.

senses.gloss_en: to speak, to talk, to utter, to say
to speak, to propose, to talk

more.definition: to speak; to talk (to say words out loud); to communicate by any means; to say something
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese falar, from Latin fābulārī (“chat, converse”). Doublet of fabular, which was borrowed from Latin. Compare Galician falar, Spanish hablar.

more.definition: little of something; a short while
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pouco, from Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare Galician pouco and Spanish poco.

more.definition: hair (filament which grows on the skin of mammals), except hair on top of humans’ heads, which is called cabelo; hair; fur (an animal’s hair as a whole)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pelo, from Latin pilus, from Proto-Indo-European *pil-. The retention of single Latin /l/ in intervocalic position is irregular and may be the product of analogy with the near-synonym cabelo < Latin capillus.

more.definition: only; just; merely (no more than); barely (by a small margin)
more.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ad poenam, with an additional adverbial /-s/ (compare entrementes, ultimately from Latin interim).

more.definition: male (human of masculine gender); man (adult male human); a person; a human being
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ome, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese omẽe, from Latin hominem (“a human”), from Proto-Italic *hemō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰm̥mṓ (“an earthling”).

more.definition: nor; and not (introduces a further negative statement); nor (introducing each except the first term of a series, indicating none of them is true)
more.etymology: Latin necder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nen, from Latin nec. Compare Galician nin, Catalan, French, and Spanish ni, Italian né.

more.definition: two (cardinal number 2)
more.etymology: Alteration of dous, from Old Galician-Portuguese dous, from Latin duōs (“two”), from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.

more.definition: place (a location or position); available room; place (a position within a rank)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logar, from Late Latin locālem (“local”), from Latin locus (“place”), from Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put”). Compare Galician lugar, Fala lugal, Asturian llugar, and Spanish lugar. Doublet of local.

more.definition: there (close to the second person (you)); towards the second person; then (soon afterwards)
more.etymology: From Latin ad (“to, toward, at”) + ibī (“there”). Compare Galician aí, Spanish ahí.

more.definition: outside (on the outside of a building or location); abroad; overseas (in another country); out (away from home or one’s usual place)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fora, from Latin forās (“outside”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door; gate”).

more.definition: to be (indicates location in space); to be (denotes a transient quality; a quality expected to change); to be; forms the progressive aspect
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese estar, from Latin stāre (“stand”). The stems estev- or estiv- found in some inflections likely come from Vulgar Latin *stēvī (perfect in -ēv-, used by some Latin second conjugation verbs), hypothetical perfect stem that displaced original Classical Latin perfect stetī. Compare the same development in Spanish estar.

more.definition: which (what one)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese qual, from Latin quālis (“which”).

more.definition: job (economic role for which a person is paid); job; task (piece of work done as part of one’s duties); work; toil; labour; effort
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese traballo (“pain, effort, labor”), deverbal from traballar (modern trabalhar).

more.definition: today (in the current day); nowadays (in the current era)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese oge (“today”), from Latin hodiē (“today”), from hōc (“this”) + diē (“day”). Cognate with Galician hoxe, Spanish hoy, Catalan avui, French hui and Italian oggi.

more.definition: no one; nobody (not one person)
more.etymology: From Latin nec (“not any”) + quem (“whom”).

more.definition: recently made or created; not previously worn or used; recently discovered
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese novo, from Latin novum (“new”), from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. Compare Galician novo and Spanish nuevo.

more.definition: world (the Universe); world (the Earth); world; humanity (human beings collectively)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mundo, from Latin mundus (“world”).

more.definition: knowledge; lore (intellectual understanding)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese saber, from Latin sapere (“taste, know”). The verb’s first-person singular conjugation reflects an original */ˈsajo/, in common with other Romance languages, of uncertain origin. The present subjunctive forms show consonant metathesis: sapiām > */ˈsajpa/ > Portuguese saiba.

more.definition: to be aware, to know; to be aware of a value or piece of information; to know how
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese saber, from Latin sapere (“taste, know”). The verb’s first-person singular conjugation reflects an original */ˈsajo/, in common with other Romance languages, of uncertain origin. The present subjunctive forms show consonant metathesis: sapiām > */ˈsajpa/ > Portuguese saiba.

more.definition: to transfer one’s possession of something to someone without anything in return; to hand over (to pass something into someone’s hand); to make a present or gift of
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dar (“to give”), from Latin dare, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).

examples.text: Eles moram em uma cidade grande.

translations.de: Sie wohnen in einer großen Stadt.
translations.en: They live in a big city.
translations.fr: Ils habitent dans une grande ville.

examples.text: Esta camisa é grande demais para mim.

translations.de: Dieses Hemd ist mir zu groß.
translations.en: This shirt is too big for me.
translations.fr: Cette chemise est trop grande pour moi.

more.definition: large; great; big (of great size or extent); large; big; numerous (numerically large); great (of great importance)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese grande, from Latin grandis, of uncertain origin.

more.definition: money (means of exchange and measure of value); a coin used from the 12th to the 15th century in Portugal
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese dĩeiro (a coin of little value), from Vulgar Latin *dīnārius, an alteration of Latin dēnārius (“small Roman silver coin”). Doublet of denário and dinar.

more.definition: name (word or phrase which identifies an individual person, place, class, or thing); name (what somebody is known for); noun
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese nome, from Latin nōmen (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

more.definition: equivalent to a third- or second-person possessive pronoun
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese lle, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese li, from Latin illī, dative of ille. Cognate with Old Spanish ge, Sicilian ci (dative), and Italian gli (dative).

more.definition: ours (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of us, excluding the person(s) being addressed); ours (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of us, including the person(s) being addressed); ours (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of any entity that the speaker is a part of or identifies with)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nosso, from Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

more.definition: son (male offspring); child (offspring of any sex); term of address for a younger male; son
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filho (“son”), from Latin fīlius (“son”), from Old Latin fīlios (“son”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Compare Galician fillo, Spanish hijo and Sicilian figghiu.

more.definition: certainty (state of being certain); something which is certain
more.etymology: From certo (“certain; sure”) + -eza, from Old Galician-Portuguese certo, from Latin certus (“certain, fixed”).

more.definition: hour (period of sixty minutes); time (point in time)
more.etymology: Ancient Greek ὥρᾱ (hṓrā)bor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ora, from Latin hōra. Doublet of ora.

more.definition: alternative letter-case form of OK

senses.gloss_en: to go out, to go places

more.definition: to exit; to leave (go away from a certain place or situation); to get out (of); to go out (leave one’s abode to go to public places); to leave (stop being involved with)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sair, from Latin salīre (“to leap”), from Proto-Indo-European *sl̥-ye-. Compare Galician saír and Spanish salir.

more.definition: problem (difficulty that has to be resolved or dealt with); problem (question to be answered); disorder (physical or psychical malfunction)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *próder. Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-der. Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma)bor. Latin problēmalbor. Learned borrowing from Latin problēma, borrowed from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”).

more.definition: thank you
hello; hi (greeting)
more.etymology: Possibly borrowed from Spanish hola (“hello”).

more.definition: kind; sort; type (grouping based on shared characteristics); type (letter or character used for printing); a language type in typology
more.etymology: From Latin typus (“figure; type”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to poke”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-.

more.definition: truly, really, actually
more.etymology: From real + -mente.

more.definition: woman (adult female human); wife; woman (noun sense 4)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese muller, moller (hence also Galician muller), from Latin mulierem (“woman; wife”), of uncertain origin. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (milk; to milk). Cognate with Mirandese mulhier, Spanish mujer, Catalan muller, Italian moglie, and Romanian muiere.

more.definition: some, any
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese algũu, from Vulgar Latin *alicūnus, from Latin aliquis + ūnus. Compare Spanish alguno, French aucun, Italian alcuno.

more.definition: great; excellent (very good); optimal (the best possible solution of a problem)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin optimus (superlative of bonus, literally “best”), from ops (“power to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”).

more.definition: cart (vehicle drawn or pushed by a person or animal); car; automobile; any “vehicle” which is drawn, such as an elevator, a cable car, or a train wagon
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese carro (“cart”), from Latin carrus, from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós, from *ḱers- (“to run”).

more.definition: friend (person whose company one enjoys); friend (an associate or thing which provides assistance); a state with good relations with another state
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese amigo, from Latin amīcus (“friend; friendly”), from amō (“to love”) + -icus. Compare Catalan amic, French ami, Italian amico, Romanian amic and Spanish amigo.

more.definition: first (before all others); first of all (used to introduce the first of a series of remarks, often with an angry tone)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese primeiro, from Latin prīmārius (“one of the first”), from prīmus (“first”). Doublet of primário and premiê. By surface analysis, primo + -eiro.

more.definition: three (cardinal number 3)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese tres, from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.

more.definition: among (denotes a mingling or intermixing with distinct or separable objects); between (in the separating position or interval); between (intermediate in quantity or degree)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entre, antre, from Latin inter (“between; among”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁enter (“between”).

more.definition: serious; solemn (without humor or expression of happiness); serious (needing great attention; leaving no room for play); dangerous
more.etymology: Latin sēriuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin sērius (“serious”).

more.definition: to return; to come back; to return (to reach a previous state); to turn (to adjust something in a direction)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *welH-der. Latin volvereder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese voltar, from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, from Latin volvere.

more.definition: part; section; portion; party (law)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parte, from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.

more.definition: love; honey, babe, sweetheart, darling (term of endearing); a kind or humble person
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₃emh₃-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese amor, from Latin amōrem. Doublet of amore.

more.definition: happy; fortunate
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese feliz, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin fēlīcem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-lw-i, from *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suckle”). The Old Galician-Portuguese form fiiz, however, was popularly inherited, but later replaced by feliz, in a process of restoration.

more.definition: although (used with subjunctive, introducing a clause that expresses a concession)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese emboora, univerbation of en boa ora.

more.definition: family; nuclear family (a father, mother and their sons and daughters); family; bloodline; kin; family
more.etymology: Latin familialbor. Learned borrowing from Latin familia (“household, family”).

senses.gloss_en: to abandon, to leave, to quit, to forsake
to cease, to stop, to quit

more.definition: to leave; to exit (to go out of or away from a place); to leave (to refrain from taking); to leave, to leave behind (to cause to exist after its occurrence)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese leixar, from Latin laxāre (“to extend; to lighten; to relax; to release”), from laxus (“loose”). Doublet of the borrowed laxar. Compare Galician deixar, Asturian dexar, and Spanish dejar, all also undergoing the shift of initial -l- to -d-. It may have been influenced by the preposition de or come from contraction of a Late Latin *dēlaxāre.

more.definition: behind (at the back); after (looking for); ago (in the past)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atras (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin *ad trans, from Latin trāns (“beyond”).

regional_variants.note: Portugal puts the pronoun after the verb: ajudar-me.

examples.text: Você pode me ajudar, por favor?

translations.de: Kannst du mir bitte helfen?
translations.en: Can you help me, please?
translations.fr: Peux-tu m'aider, s'il te plaît ?

examples.text: Ele ajudou a irmã com a mudança.

translations.de: Er hat seiner Schwester beim Umzug geholfen.
translations.en: He helped his sister with the move.
translations.fr: Il a aidé sa sœur à déménager.

more.definition: to help, aid; to assist
collocations: dar uma mão — to lend a hand
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ajudar, from Latin adiūtāre. Compare Asturian ayudar, Catalan ajudar, Ladino ayudar, Occitan ajudar, Spanish ayudar.

more.definition: that over there, yon (far from the speaker and the listener)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aquele, from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from Latin eccum + ille. Cognate with Spanish aquel.

more.definition: side
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese lado, from Latin lātus. Compare Spanish lado and Italian lato.

more.definition: shit; faeces (excretory product evacuated from the bowels); a chunk of shit; shit (rubbish; worthless matter)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese merda, from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).

more.definition: late (near the end of a period of time); late (specifically, near the end of the day); late (not arriving until after an expected time)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese tarde, from Latin tardē (“tardily; late”, adverb), from tardus (“late”, adjective). Compare French tard, Spanish tarde and related to English tardy.

more.definition: afternoon
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese tarde, from Latin tardē (“tardily; late”, adverb), from tardus (“late”, adjective). Compare French tard, Spanish tarde and related to English tardy.

more.definition: taste (one of the five senses); taste, flavour (a sensation produced by the tongue); taste (a person's implicit set of preferences, especially aesthetic)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese gosto, from Latin gustus, from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.

more.definition: if (introduces a condition)
more.etymology: Latin cāsuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin cāsus.

more.definition: an actual event, situation or fact; piece of work to be done; instance used as a topic of study
more.etymology: Latin cāsuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin cāsus.

more.definition: inside (within or into something’s interior); indoors (in a building)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁énterosder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dentro, from Late Latin dē intrō.

more.definition: city, town; city life, urban life
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cidade, from Latin cīvitātem.

more.definition: moment (very brief period of time); momentum
more.etymology: Latin mōmentumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin mōmentum.

senses.gloss_en: to get, to receive, to be given
to come down with, to have, to get
to get, to obtain, to procure, to provide with

more.definition: to grab, hold; to discover someone doing something; to pick up
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin picāre (“smear with pitch”), from pix (“pitch”).

more.definition: a group of two or more persons; persons forming a distinct identity; guys, folks (informal address to a group of people)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese gente, from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tim.

more.definition: tomorrow (in the day after today)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese a mannãa (literally "at morning", in a similar sense to English tomorrow) from Vulgar Latin *māneāna. Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese cras.

more.definition: head (part of the body); head (topmost, foremost, or leading part); sense
more.etymology: Latin -iusnom. From Old Galician-Portuguese cabeça, from Vulgar Latin capitia, from the neuter plural (reanalyzed as a feminine singular) of Latin capitium, from caput.

more.definition: badly (in a faulty, dysfunctional or incorrect manner); hardly; barely; wrong (incorrect)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mal, from Latin male (“badly; wrongly”).

more.definition: as; while (at the same time as); while; whereas (introduces a situation that is contrasts with another situation)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enquanto, from en (“in”) + quanto (“how much”). Compare Spanish en cuanto.

more.definition: soon (in a short while); immediately after, right after; already (used to emphasize impatience)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logo, from Latin locō (“in the place of, instead of, for”, ablative), from Old Latin stlocus, from Proto-Indo-European *stel- (“to put, place, locate”). Compare Galician logo and Spanish luego. Doublet of lócus.

more.definition: since; from
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese des (“since”) + de (“of”).

more.definition: girl, female equivalent of garoto
person (an individual being, especially a human); person (someone’s physical body); person (either the speaker, those spoken to or the subject of the discussion)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pessõa, from Latin persōna (“mask used by actor; role, part, character”), perhaps a loanword from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu, “mask”), from Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon). Doublet of persona.

more.definition: legal; cool, nice, good
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis (“legal”), from lēx (“law”). Doublet of leal.

more.definition: fast (occurring or happening within a short time)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Latin rapiduslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin rapidus.

more.definition: each, every (qualifying a singular noun, indicating all examples of the thing so named seen as individual or separate items); used as an intensifier
more.etymology: Ancient Greek κατά (katá)bor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cada, from Latin cata (“by”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κατά (katá).

more.definition: half
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese meio, meo, from Latin medius, from Proto-Italic *meðios, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare the borrowed doublets médio and médium. Sense of "way" or "mean" from Latin medium.

more.definition: fear (emotion caused by actual or perceived danger or threat)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese medo, from Latin metus (“fear”). Compare Spanish miedo.

more.definition: brother (male sibling); sibling (person having the same parents as another); brother (member of a brotherhood)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmão (“brother”), from Latin germānus (“brother”), from the adjective germānus (“of true siblings”), from germen (“sprout, bud”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁mn̥ (“offspring, seed”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget, to give birth”). Cognates include Galician irmán, Mirandese armano, Asturian hermanu, and Spanish hermano.

more.definition: not correct; wrong; incorrect
more.etymology: Past participle of errar.

more.definition: history; story
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin historia (“history”), from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, “learning through research, narration of what is learned”), from ἱστορέω (historéō, “to learn through research, to inquire”), from ἵστωρ (hístōr, “the one who knows, the expert, the judge”). Doublet of estória and story.

more.definition: almost (very close to)
more.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin quasi (“as if”). Cognate of Spanish casi, Spanish cuasi, French quasi and Italian quasi.

more.definition: to meet; to find; to locate; to be located
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese encontrar, from Vulgar Latin *incontrāre, from Latin in + contrā. Compare Italian incontrare, Old French encontrer, Spanish encontrar.

more.definition: personal
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin persōnālis.

more.definition: difficult, hard, unlikely
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin difficilis. See dificuldade for more.

more.definition: form; shape (the visible structure of a thing); shape; figure (a geometric object); form (a conventional method way of doing something)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fōrma. Doublet of etymology 2, which was inherited.

more.definition: against
more.etymology: Proto-Italic *komterosder. Inherited from Latin contrā.

more.definition: to kill (to cause to die); to kill; to eradicate; to destroy; to kill (to cause extreme pain, distress or exhaustion in)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese matar, probably from Latin mactāre (through Vulgar Latin *mattāre). The development of -ct- would be irregular, however. Hence possibly derived from or influenced by Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), related to madidus. Another possibility is an influence by Arabic مَاتَ (māta, “to die”).

more.definition: week (period of seven days)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese semana, from Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), from septimus (“seventh”).

more.definition: close, closely, next (at a little distance)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese preto, from earlier *apreto, from apretar (Modern Portuguese apertar), from Late Latin appectorāre, from Latin pectus. Doublet of preto. Cognate of Galician preto.

more.definition: help, assistance, aid; an act of helping or assisting; something which helps or assists
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ajuda, from ajudar (“to help; to aid”), from Latin adiūtāre (“to help”). Compare English aid, Spanish ayuda, Italian aiuto and Occitan ajuda.

more.definition: year
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ano (“year”), from Latin annus (“year”), from Proto-Italic *atnos (“year”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-nos-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”). Cognate with Galician ano, Spanish año, Catalan any, Occitan, French, and Romanian an, Italian anno.

more.definition: path; way, route; means
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caminho, from Late Latin cammīnus (“way”), from Gaulish. Compare Galician camiño.

more.definition: they (a group of people other than the speaker, entirely female); third-person feminine plural personal pronoun used in all positions; they; them; it
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ellas, from Latin illās, accusative feminine plural of ille.

more.definition: morning
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mannãa (“morning”), from Vulgar Latin *maneāna (“morning”), from Latin māne (“in the morning”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, to mature”). Cognate with Galician mañá, Asturian mañana, Leonese mañana, Mirandese manhana, Spanish mañana, and Aragonese manyana.

more.definition: fate; luck
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sorte, from Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish suerte.

more.definition: death (cessation of life); the state of being dead; destruction; ruin
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese morte, from Latin mortem (“death”), from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).

governs.meaning: to reflect on, hold an opinion

senses.gloss_en: to think something over, to consider, to ponder, to contemplate

regional_variants.note: Portugal uses tu: o que pensas?

examples.text: Eu penso muito na minha família.

translations.de: Ich denke oft an meine Familie.
translations.en: I often think of my family.
translations.fr: Je pense souvent à ma famille.

examples.text: O que você pensa sobre este livro?

translations.de: Was denkst du über dieses Buch?
translations.en: What do you think about this book?
translations.fr: Que penses-tu de ce livre ?

more.definition: to think (communicate to oneself in one’s mind); to conceive, intend
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre. Doublet of pesar.

more.definition: dad, papa
more.etymology: Portuguese pairedup. Reduplication of pai.

senses.gloss_en: over there, on the other side

more.definition: there (far from both the speaker and the interlocutor(s))
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ali, aly, from Vulgar Latin *adlic, from Latin ad (“to”) + illīc (“there”).

more.definition: quarter; fourth (one of four parts of a whole); room (subdivision within a building); bedroom (room used to sleep in and keep personal objects)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese quarto, from Latin quārtus.

more.definition: to take (to move something to a destination); to take away (to remove someone or something from the current location); to take out (to get food from an eatery to be eaten elsewhere)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese levar, from Latin levāre. Compare Galician levar, Spanish llevar, French lever, Italian levare, Romanian luare.

more.definition: daughter
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese filha (“daughter”), from Latin fīlia (“daughter”), from fīlius (“son”). Compare Galician filla.

more.definition: dead (no longer living); dead (completely inactive); exhausted (extremely tired)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese morto, from Vulgar Latin *mortu(s), from Latin mortuus, perfect active participle of morior (“to die”). Corresponds to Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, *mr̥tós (“dead, mortal”), *mr̥tó-, ultimately from *mer- (“to die”). Compare Galician morto and Spanish muerto.

more.definition: door; entrance; gateway
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porta, from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).

senses.gloss_en: to achieve, to accomplish, to attain, to acquire

more.definition: to arrive (at); to reach (to conclude moving to a destination); to arrive (to reach the present time); to reach (to extend to as far as)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chegar, apheresis of Latin applicāre. Compare Galician chegar and Spanish llegar. See also the doublets pregar and plicar.

more.definition: water (H₂O); water (a serving of water); water (water in a body)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese agua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with Galician auga, Spanish agua, Catalan aigua, Occitan aiga, French eau, Italian acqua and Romanian apă.

more.definition: ready, finished; fast; instant; immediate (that does not delay); fit, prepared
more.etymology: Latin prōmptuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin prōmptus. Doublet of prompt.
Latin spōnsusnom. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esposa, from Latin spōnsa.

senses.gloss_en: to come, to arrive, to advance, to return

more.definition: to come (to move towards the speaker or the agent); to come; to arrive (to reach a destination, especially where the speaker is); to come (to manifest itself; to occur)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese viir~vĩir, from Latin venīre. The sense of “to achieve orgasm” is probably a semantic loan from English come.

more.definition: to hear (to perceive with the ear, without necessarily paying attention to it); to pay attention to; to take into account, take into consideration
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ouvyr, oyr, from earlier ouir, from Latin audīre, a compound of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”)) and *dʰh₁-ye/o- (“to render”). Cognate with Galician ouvir, Spanish oír, Catalan oir, Occitan ausir, French ouïr, Italian udire and Romanian auzi.

senses.gloss_en: to die, to perish, to decease, to depart

more.definition: to die (to stop living); to die; to break down (to stop working); to be dead to (to lose all social ties with)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese morrer, morer, from Latin morī (via a de-deponentized *morĕre).

more.definition: boy, young man; café au lait, latte (coffee with milk)
more.etymology: Unknown. Maybe related to French gars.

more.definition: heart (organ of the body); heart, emotions, kindness, spirit; center, core
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese coraçon, from Vulgar Latin *corāceōnem, derived from Latin cor, from Proto-Italic *kord, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr ~ *ḱr̥d-. Compare Galician and Spanish corazón, Mozarabic ڧرجون (qurəjūn).

more.definition: to tell (to convey given information); to tell; to narrate (relate a story or series of events); to count (determine the quantity of)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese contar, from Latin computāre. Doublet of computar.

more.definition: important (having relevant and crucial value); influential
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin importantem (“importing; causing”). By surface analysis, importar + -ante.

more.definition: play; game; sport; gaming
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jogo, from Latin iocum. Compare Galician xogo and Spanish juego.

more.definition: reason (the ability to think correctly); reason; motive (the cause of an action or determination); correctness; rightness (the condition of being right)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese razon, from Latin ratiōnem. Doublet of ração and rácio.

more.definition: idea (that which comes to mind); plan, project; objective, conception or conviction that is based on something
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *weyd-der. Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa)der. Latin idealbor. Learned borrowing from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”).

more.definition: idiotic
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

more.definition: idiot
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

more.definition: to pass; to pass by (to move past); to overtake (to move ahead of); to cross (to move beyond)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-der. Latin -ereinflu. English passsl. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese passar. Verb sense 17 is a semantic loan from English pass. Compare Galician and Spanish pasar.

senses.gloss_en: to stop, to quit, to give up

more.definition: to stop (to no longer move); to stop (to no longer progress or do something); to stop (to cause something to no longer move)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese parar, from Latin parāre (“to prepare”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth”).

more.definition: lady; mistress
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sénosder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese senhor.

more.definition: end, conclusion, closure
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fim, fin, from Latin finis, of disputed origin. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- or Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd-.

more.definition: body; corpse, cadaver; any limited amount of matter
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese corpo, from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowings corpus and cós.

more.definition: chief, head, head man, boss; chieftain; chef (the head cook of an establishment such as a restaurant)
more.etymology: Borrowed from French chef; cognates include Spanish jefe and English chief. Doublet of chef, cabo, and caput.

more.definition: power (the ability to coerce, influence or control); power (a powerful organization, especially a country); power (branch of the government)
more.etymology: Nominalization of Etymology 1.

more.definition: to be able to; can (to have the ability to); can; to be allowed to (to have the permission to); can; could (indicates possibility)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese poder, from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

more.definition: mum, mom, mummy
more.etymology: From mãe.

senses.gloss_en: to begin, to start, to commence

more.definition: to start; to begin; to commence; to begin; to start to do; to start; to initiate (to cause something to begin)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese começar, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, from com- + Latin initiāre. Compare Galician comezar. It has been supposed that the Portuguese form developed via an unattested *comẽeçar, but this appears unlikely. The loss of /n/ was likely due to analogy with the synonym empeçar (cf. Spanish comenzar, diphthongally influenced by empezar).

more.definition: weapon
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arma, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”). Compare Galician arma.

more.definition: distant, faraway
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese longe, from Latin longe.

more.definition: far, a long way
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese longe, from Latin longe.

more.definition: school (institution dedicated to teaching and learning); school (an art movement); school (the followers of a particular doctrine)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese escola, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “spare time, leisure”). The Portuguese form may indicate a semi-learned influence on the phonetic aspects of the word.

more.definition: to try, go for, attempt; to tease, tempt; to dare, challenge
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tentar, from Latin temptāre.

more.definition: so; then (in that case); emphasises a yes-or-no answer or an order
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pois, from Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post (“after”). Compare with French puis, Spanish pues, Italian poi, and Romanian apoi (from ad post).

more.definition: because; for (by or for the cause that)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pois, from Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post (“after”). Compare with French puis, Spanish pues, Italian poi, and Romanian apoi (from ad post).

more.definition: land; region; territory (area associated with something); ground (the surface of the Earth outside buildings); land; property (partitioned and measurable area owned by someone)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese terra, from Latin terra.

more.definition: yesterday
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese oonte (“yesterday”), from *ãoite, from earlier *anoite, from Latin ad noctem (“towards the night”), from nox (“night”). Displaced Old Galician-Portuguese eire. Cognate with Galician onte and Spanish anoche.

more.definition: cause, reason; suit, lawsuit; goal, aim
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin causa. Doublet of the inherited coisa and cousa. Cognates include English and French cause, Italian and Spanish causa.

more.definition: war (organised, large-scale armed conflict); war; warfare (the waging of war); war (any large-scale conflict)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese guerra, from Early Medieval Latin werra, borrowed from Frankish *werʀu, from Proto-West Germanic *werʀan + *-u.. Related to the word varrer.

more.definition: probability; chance, opportunity
more.etymology: French chancebor. Borrowed from French chance. Doublet of cadência.

more.definition: to use; to utilise; to employ; to make use of; to sport (to wear, wield or have as a notable feature); to use (to consume habitually)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese usar, from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre.

more.definition: husband (male partner in a married couple)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese marido, from Latin marītus (“husband”), from mās (“male, a male”).

more.definition: hand; forefoot (either of the front feet of a quadruped); hand (a round of a card game)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mão (“hand”), from Latin manus (“hand”), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry). Cognate with Galician man, Spanish mano, Catalan mà, Occitan man, French main, Italian mano and Romanian mână.

more.definition: to work (to do a specific task)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese traballar, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”). Compare Galician traballar, Spanish trabajar. By surface analysis, trabalho + -ar.

more.definition: blood (vital liquid flowing in human and animal bodies); blood (family relationship due to birth, e.g. between siblings)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sangue, sangui, from Latin sanguinem m, from older sanguen, from *san-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare Galician sangue m, Spanish sangre f, Italian sangue m, French sang m.

more.definition: music (melodic and rhythmic sounds made as art); song (any musical composition); music; musicology (the study of music)
more.etymology: Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ)bor. Latin mūsicalbor. Learned borrowing from Latin mūsica, borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”). By surface analysis, musa + -ica.

senses.gloss_en: to await, to expect, to abide

translations.en: I am waiting for the bus.
translations.fr: J'attends le bus.

examples.text: Esperamos uma hora por você.

translations.de: Wir haben eine Stunde auf dich gewartet.
translations.en: We waited an hour for you.
translations.fr: Nous t'avons attendu pendant une heure.

more.definition: to wait (for); to await; to wait; to hope for (to really want)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asperar, from Latin spērāre, from Old Latin *spēsō, from spēs (“hope”) + -ō (verbal suffix).

more.definition: odd; strange (not normal); unknown; unfamiliar (not known or familiar)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estranho, from Latin extrāneus. Cognates include Spanish extraño, Catalan estrany, French étrange and Italian strano.

more.definition: old; ancient (having existed for a long period of time); old; aged (having lived for most of the expected years); old (that has been used for a considerable period of time)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese velho, from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

more.definition: mouth (the opening of a creature through which food is ingested); mouth (the end of a river out of which water flows into a sea or other large body of water); brim (of a bottle or any other container)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese boca, from Latin bucca, of Celtic origin.

more.definition: party; celebration; festival
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese festa, from Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstum.

more.definition: speech (the ability to speak); something spoken, such as a phrase or line; a way of speaking
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fala, from Latin fābula (“discourse, narrative”). Doublet of fábula, a learned borrowing.

senses.gloss_en: to get, to receive, to be given
to detach, to remove, to extirpate, to deprive

more.definition: to take, take out, take away; to remove, withdraw; to get, obtain (a score or document)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *der-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tirar, from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

more.definition: to consume meals; to consume a specific food; to eat some
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese comer, from Vulgar Latin *comēre, restructuring of Latin comedere. Cognate with Galician, Mirandese, Asturian, and Spanish comer and Mirandese quemer.

more.definition: easy (requiring little skill or effort); which is understood at no cost; simple; who has an affable attitude; accessible
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin facilis, from faciō (“to do; to make”), whence fazer.

more.definition: again (having already happened before)
more.etymology: From nova + -mente.

more.definition: sister
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese irmãa, yrmãa, from Latin germāna (“sister”), from the adjective germānus (“of siblings”); more at irmão. By surface analysis, irmão + -a (forms feminine equivalents).

more.definition: sufficient; enough
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sufficientem, present participle of sufficiō.

more.definition: parents
second (¹⁄₆₀ of a minute); second (extremely short period of time); the second one (something that comes immediately after the first)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese segundo, from Latin secundus, probably taken as a semi-learned term.

more.definition: according to (based on what is stated by)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese segundo, from Latin secundus, probably taken as a semi-learned term.

more.definition: five
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese cinco~cinquo~cinque, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, from Latin quīnque. Distantly, a doublet of ponche.

more.definition: dear; lovely, cute
more.etymology: Past participle of querer. Displaced expected *quesido.

more.definition: sweetheart; darling
more.etymology: Past participle of querer. Displaced expected *quesido.

more.definition: pre-reform spelling (used until 1990) of ideia; may still occur as a sporadic misspelling
number (quantity); number (entity used to describe quantity); number (element of mathematical set)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese número, from Latin numerus.

senses.gloss_en: to make, to manage, to accomplish, to complete
to get, to obtain, to procure, to provide with

more.definition: to get, obtain; to achieve; to be able to, can
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *cōnsequīre or cōnsequere, from Latin cōnsequī. By surface analysis, con- (“co-”) + seguir (“to follow”).

more.definition: to take (to get something into one’s possession or control); to take; to conquer (to seize control of a location); to steal (to take something illegally)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tomar, of unknown origin. Compare Galician and Spanish tomar.

more.definition: enough; sufficiently; rather; fairly; quite
more.etymology: From bastar (“to be enough”) + -ante.

more.definition: manner; way (particular method of doing something); the specific style of an artist; appearance; look; aspect; guise
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese maneira, from Vulgar Latin *manāria, from feminine of Latin manuārius (“relating to the hand”), from manus (“hand”); corresponding to mão + -eira. Compare Galician maneira, Spanish and Catalan manera, French manière, English manner, Romanian mâner.

more.definition: four
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese quatro, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwṓr.

more.definition: to happen; to occur; to take place; to become famous or successful
more.etymology: Vulgar Latin *contigīreder. Derived from Vulgar Latin *contigīre, from Latin contingere. Compare Galician acontecer and Spanish acontecer.

examples.text: A criança está brincando no parque.

translations.de: Das Kind spielt im Park.
translations.en: The child is playing in the park.
translations.fr: L'enfant joue dans le parc.

examples.text: As crianças estão na escola.

translations.de: Die Kinder sind in der Schule.
translations.en: The children are at school.
translations.fr: Les enfants sont à l'école.

more.definition: child (young person)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese criança. By surface analysis, criar (“to raise”) + -ança. Compare Spanish crianza and Medieval Latin creantia.

usage_note: Always feminine, also for a boy.

more.definition: to sleep; to be asleep (to rest in a state of reduced consciousness); to fall asleep (to become asleep); to have a given type of sleep
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dormir, from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

more.definition: during (for all of a given time interval); during (at any point within a given time interval); for (introduces the duration of an occurrence)
more.etymology: From Latin dūrantem (“enduring”), from dūrō (“last, endure”), from dūrus (“hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *deru-, *drew- (“hard, fest”).

more.definition: coffee (beverage); coffee (a serving of this beverage); coffee bean
more.etymology: Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa)bor. Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve)bor. Italian caffèbor. French cafébor. Borrowed from French café, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve) (Turkish kahve), from Classical Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa, “coffee”).

more.definition: possible; potential; likely
more.etymology: Latin possibilislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin possibilis.

more.definition: wedding (marriage ceremony); marriage
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese casamento, from casar (“marry”). By surface analysis, casar + -mento.

more.definition: team
more.etymology: Borrowed from French équipe (“team”), from équiper (“to equip”).

more.definition: bad; unpleasant; evil
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₃rew-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roin, ultimately from Latin ruīna or a word from the same root. Compare Galician ruín, Spanish ruin, Catalan roí, French ruine.

more.definition: fault; guilt
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin culpa.

more.definition: probably
more.etymology: From provável + -mente.

more.definition: telephone; telephone number
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *kʷelh₁-der. Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle)lbor. Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-der. Ancient Greek φωνή (phōnḗ)der. French téléphonebor. English telephonebor. French téléphonebor. Borrowed from English telephone or French téléphone. By surface analysis, tele- + -fone.

more.definition: capable of producing great force; strong; forceful; capable of withstanding great force; strong; durable; highly stimulating to the senses; intense; extreme; strong
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese forte.

more.definition: to sense; to feel (to perceive by means of biological senses); to feel (to feel with the skin or hands); to feel (to experience an emotion or feeling [noun])
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentir, from Latin sentīre, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”).

senses.gloss_en: to live, to lodge, to reside, to dwell

more.definition: to live; to have life; to live, reside (have permanent residence); to keep, continue for a long period of time
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese viver, from Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti.

more.definition: alone; by oneself; on one's own
more.etymology: From só (“alone”) + -zinho (forms certain augmentatives).

more.definition: pleasure
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prazer, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin placēre. Compare Spanish placer and Galician pracer. (interjection): Ellipsis of phrases such as é um prazer conhecê-lo/la (“it’s a pleasure to meet you”).

more.definition: question
more.etymology: Deverbal from perguntar.

more.definition: minute (60 seconds)
more.etymology: Latin minūtuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin minūtus. Compare the inherited doublet miúdo. Also doublet of menu, via French.
