more.definition: room (division in a building); ellipsis of sala de estar (“living room”); ellipsis of sala de aula (“classroom”)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sala, from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *salą. Doublet of Sá.

more.definition: unique; only, single, sole
more.etymology: Latin ūnicuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin ūnicus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aquilo, from Vulgar Latin *eccum illum, neuter singular of *eccum ille.

more.definition: noncredible, uncredible; incredible, amazing; incredible, wonderful
more.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin incrēdibilis or adapted based on crível. By surface analysis, in- + crível. Piecewise doublet of incredível. Cognate with Galician incríbel, Spanish increíble, Catalan increïble, French incroyable, Occitan incredible, Italian incredibile, and English incredible.

more.definition: law (body of rules and standards to be applied by courts)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Modified orthographically from Old Galician-Portuguese dereito (compare Spanish derecho), from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus, from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of direto.

more.definition: to change (to become or cause to become something different); to move, to relocate (to settle into a new home)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mudar, from Latin mūtāre. Doublet of mutar.

more.definition: to lose (an object, a job, interest etc.); to lose (to be defeated in a match, an election etc.); to miss (an opportunity, a train or bus etc.)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese perder, from Latin perdere. The first person singular form in the present indicative and all forms of the present subjunctive and commands (except the second person informal affirmative commands) have an analogous change from D to C (expected "perdo" instead of "perco," for example).

more.definition: security; safety (condition of not being threatened); any object related to the safety of something or some place; a set of devices designed to help avoid surprise attacks
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese segurança. By surface analysis, segurar (“to hold; to secure”) + -ança.

more.definition: to give [someone] money in exchange for a good or service; (to give money in order to discharge [a debt or bill]); to pay for; to buy (to give money in exchange for [a good or service])
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pagar, from Latin pacāre (“to pacify”).

more.definition: plane (level or flat surface); plane (flat surface extending infinitely in all directions); plan (set of intended actions)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin plānus (“flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-. Doublet of chão, porão, lhano, and piano.

senses.gloss_en: to find out, to discover, to figure out, to learn

more.definition: to discover (to find something for the first time); to find out; to uncover (to remove something’s cover)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese descobrir (“to find out”), from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperīre (“to expose”), from Latin dis- + cooperiō (“to cover wholly”). By surface analysis, des- + cobrir.

more.definition: to find; to encounter (to come across something that was unknown or had been lost); to find; to consider (to have the opinion that a given thing has the given quality); to find (to come across something in the given state)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₁-der. Proto-Italic *flāōder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese achar, from Latin afflāre. Compare Galician achar and Spanish hallar.

more.definition: food, something edible; meal
more.etymology: From the past participle of comer (“to eat”).

more.definition: young, youthful
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis, from Proto-Italic *juwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwHō (“young”). Compare Galician xove, Spanish joven.

senses.gloss_en: to look, to gaze, to view, to see

more.definition: to look
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese aollar, from Vulgar Latin *adoculāre, from oclus, from Latin oculus. Cognate with Galician ollar, Mirandese oulhar, Spanish aojar and Italian adocchiare.

more.definition: bed (furniture for sleeping on)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cama, from Late Latin cama, first attested in Isidore. Likely a borrowing from an Iberian substrate.

more.definition: point, a specific spot, location, or place; point, a unit of scoring; point, a topic of discussion
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ponto, from Latin punctum (“point”), from pungō (“to prick, to puncture, to punch”). Cognate with Spanish punto. Doublet of point.

more.definition: past (of the past); last; previous (nouns modified by passado in this sense can be noun phrases or adverb phrases); past its ripeness; beginning to rot
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese passado, corresponding to passar (“to pass”) + -ado.

more.definition: past (the period of time that has already happened, in contrast to the present and the future); past; past tense (verb tense expressing actions that already happened)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese passado, corresponding to passar (“to pass”) + -ado.

more.definition: punishment; pain; sadness; feather
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pena (displacing pẽa), from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂.

senses.gloss_en: to place, to put, to stand

more.definition: to place; to put; to put; to hire; to employ
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin collocāre (“to place, to put, to assemble”). Compare the inherited doublet colgar.

more.definition: goodbye; bye; see you
more.etymology: Proto-Slavic *slověninъder. Ancient Greek Σκλαβηνός (Sklabēnós)der. Medieval Greek Σκλᾰ́βος (Sklắbos)bor. Venetan s-ciao, sciavobor. Italian ciaobor. Borrowed from Italian ciao. Doublet of escravo, eslavo, esloveno, and esclavão / eslavão.

more.definition: calm; tranquility
more.etymology: From Late Latin cauma (“heat of the midday sun”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”). Possibly through the intermediate of Italian calma, although the word was found in Ibero-Romance as early as in Italian.

more.definition: film; movie; motion picture; plastic film (thin layer of plastic used to wrap objects, usually food); film
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *pel-der. English filmbor. Borrowed from English film.

more.definition: to ask for; to request (to express the need or desire for something); to order (to request a product or service); to ask for; to invite (to be in obvious need of)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pedir, from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere (“ask, request”). Compare Romanian peți, Italian pezzire.

more.definition: peace
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese paz, from Latin pācem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Compare Galician paz.

more.definition: crazy, mad, insane (of unsound mind); crazy (very unexpected; wildly surprising)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese louco, possibly from Andalusian Arabic لَوَق (lawaq, “stupidity”), from Arabic لاق (lāq, “to soften”). Compare Galician louco, Spanish loco and Sicilian loccu.

more.definition: unit of language; oath; guarantee; brief conversation
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese palavra, with hyperthesis from earlier paravra, paravla, from Late Latin parabola (“speech”), from Latin parabola (“comparison, illustration”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Doublet of parábola, a borrowing.

more.definition: here (in this place); hither (to this place); here (at this time; at the present situation)
more.etymology: Latin ecce eum (vidē)ellip. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aca, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hāc. Compare archaic French çà, Spanish acá, Italian qua and Sicilian ccà.

more.definition: small
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pequeno, possibly from Vulgar Latin *peccuinnus. Compare Spanish pequeño, French petit and Italian piccolo.

more.definition: near, close; recent; next
more.etymology: Latin proximuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin proximus. Compare Spanish prójimo.

more.definition: consulting room, clinic; remedy
more.etymology: Latin medicuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin medicus.

senses.gloss_en: to call, to call up, to give a bell, to give a call

more.definition: to link; to connect; to join (to put things together so they work together); to connect; to associate (to consider multiples things related); to turn on (to make a device start operating)
more.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin ligāre, from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”). Compare the form liar, which may have (Old) French influence, as well as the inherited Old Portuguese form legar.

more.definition: force; strength; ability to exert influence on others; authority; power; force
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese força, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“fort”). Compare Galician forza, Spanish fuerza.

senses.gloss_en: to show, to present, to indicate, to demonstrate

more.definition: to show; to show off (to demonstrate something for the purpose of bragging)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mostrar, from Latin mōnstrāre.

more.definition: country; nation (a sovereign polity); country; land (a region inhabited by a particular people or characterised by a certain feature)
more.etymology: Borrowed from French pays, from Medieval Latin pagēnsis, from Latin pāgus (“country”). Doublet of pago.

more.definition: fire (chemical reaction producing a flame); fire (destructive occurrence of fire in a certain place); house, family
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fogo, from Latin focum. Cognate with Galician fogo, Spanish fuego, Catalan foc, Occitan fuòc, French feu, Italian fuoco and Romanian foc. Doublet of foco.

more.definition: under
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sob, so, su, from Latin sub, from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo (“under, below”).

senses.gloss_en: to end, to finish, to complete, to terminate

more.definition: to finish (to be over, completed); to complete; to finish (to make done); to end up (to eventually do)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese acabar, from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare Spanish acabar, French achever and English achieve. By surface analysis, a- + cabo + -ar.

more.definition: light (medium within which vision is possible); light; light source (object that emits light); light; enlightenment (knowledge about things as they really are)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese luz, from Latin lūcem, from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“white; light; bright”). Doublet of lux. Compare Galician luz.

more.definition: to play (to participate in a sport or game); to throw; to hurl (to shove an object away); to hand (something) over by throwing
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese jogar, from Latin iocārī. Compare Galician xogar, Asturian xugar, Spanish jugar.

examples.text: Estou lendo um livro sobre história.

translations.de: Ich lese ein Buch über Geschichte.
translations.en: I am reading a book about history.
translations.fr: Je lis un livre sur l'histoire.

examples.text: Estes livros pertencem à biblioteca.

translations.de: Diese Bücher gehören der Bibliothek.
translations.en: These books belong to the library.
translations.fr: Ces livres appartiennent à la bibliothèque.

more.definition: book; omasum (third part of the stomach of ruminants, which internally has numerous folds)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese livro, an early borrowing from Latin librum. Cognate with Galician, Spanish, and Italian libro, Catalan llibre, Occitan libre and French livre.

more.definition: goodbye (farewell)
more.etymology: Old Latin deivosder. Medieval Latin ad Deumlbor. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós, Catalan adeu, Dutch ajuus, English, French, and Occitan adieu, German tschüss, Greek αντίο (antío), Galician adeus, Italian addio, Maltese addiju, Mirandese adius, Romanian adio, Serbo-Croatian ади̏о/adȉo, Slovene adȋjo.

more.definition: to keep, maintain; to hold, sustain, support; to keep (to continue doing something)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese manteer, mantẽer, from Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Compare Galician manter, Spanish mantener, French maintenir, Italian mantenere.

more.definition: early (at a time before expected; sooner than usual); early (near the start of the day)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cedo, from Latin citō.

more.definition: to want; to wish; to desire; to want; to want to (to feel the need to do something)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese querer, from Latin quaerere (“seek, look for, desire”). Compare Galician querer.

more.definition: excuse, pretext (explanation designed to avoid or alleviate guilt or negative judgement); apology (expression of remorse)
more.etymology: Deverbal from desculpar. Compare Catalan and Spanish disculpa.

more.definition: hospital
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese hospital, espital, spital, borrowed from Late Latin hospitālis (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), from Latin hospitālis (“hospitable”). Doublet of the inherited hospedal.

more.definition: six
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese seis, seys, from Latin sex (“six”), from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs (“six”).

more.definition: final; last; latest; most recent; last so far
more.etymology: Latin ultimuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin ultimus.

more.definition: to call; to summon (to ask someone to come); to call, to name (to use as the name of); to call, to label
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chamar, from Latin clāmāre (“to cry out”). Doublet of clamar, a learned borrowing. Cognate with Galician chamar, Catalan clamar, Italian chiamare and Spanish llamar.

more.definition: office (building or room); ministry; secretariat; bureau; writing desk
more.etymology: Latin -iusnom. Latin scrīptōriumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin scrīptōrium.

more.definition: king (male monarch); king (chess piece); king (playing card)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rei, from Latin rēgem (“king”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“rules”). Compare Galician and Fala rei.

more.definition: to buy
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese comprar, conprar, from Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“to prepare, to procure, to get, to purchase, to obtain”). Doublet of comparar.

more.definition: after (later in time); past (further in location); after (a great amount of)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese apos, from Latin ad post.

more.definition: the rest (that which remains); remainder; leftover (something left behind); remainder (amount left over after subtracting the divisor as many times as possible from the dividend)
more.etymology: Deverbal from restar (“to be left”), from Latin restāre, from re- + stō.

more.definition: to win (to achieve victory in a game, a war, etc); to earn (to receive payment for work)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese gãar, gaanhar. Compare Galician gañar.

more.definition: Brazilian Portuguese standard form of controlo
oneself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, yourselves, themselves
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese si, from Latin sibi, from Proto-Indo-European *sébʰye, dative of *swé (“self”). Cognate with French soi, Italian sé, Spanish sí.

more.definition: president (head of state of a republic); chairperson, chair (head of a corporate board); clipping of presidente da câmara (literally “chamber president”): mayor (head of a city)
more.etymology: Latin praesidentemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin praesidentem (“presiding over; president, leader”). By surface analysis, presidir + -ente.

senses.gloss_en: real, actual, as a matter of fact

more.definition: true, real; that has physical existence; real; being a member of the set of real numbers; real
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(H)reh₁-der. Latin reālislbor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese real, from Late Latin reālem (“actual”), from Latin rēs (“matter, thing”).

more.definition: Contraction of a + onde ("to where, whereto, whither"), used with verbs denoting movement
more.etymology: Egyptian 𓃾 (kꜣ)der. Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ)bor. Ancient Greek Α (A)bor. Etruscan 𐌀 (a)influ. Latin *cundeder. From a (“to”) + onde (“where”).

more.definition: to need; to need to, to have to, must; to be in need
more.etymology: From preciso (“necessary”) + -ar.

more.definition: affair (that which is done or is to be done); business, enterprise; thing, stuff
more.etymology: Latin negōtiumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin negōtium (“business, affair”).

more.definition: a doctor (a person who has attained a doctorate); a doctor, a physician (a member of the medical profession)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese doutor (“scholar”), a semi-learned borrowing from Latin doctōrem (“teacher”).

more.definition: eventually; at last, finally (after a long time); lastly; finally; in the end (at the conclusion)
more.etymology: From final + -mente.

more.definition: state (subdivision of a nation); status, condition, standing
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estado, from Latin status, from Proto-Italic *status, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂-tu-s ~ *sth₂-téw-s, from *steh₂- + *-tus. Doublet of status.

more.definition: foot, part of the human body; foot, part of the body of some terrestrial animals; foot (lower part of a slope)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pee, from Latin pedem. Cognate with Galician pé, Asturian and Spanish pie, and Catalan peu

more.definition: to take care (of); to look after (to provide care for); to take care; to be careful; to take care (of); to deal (with); to handle
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese cuidar, from Latin cōgitāre (“to think, to consider”), from co- + agitō (“to agitate”). Doublet of cogitar, a borrowing.

regional_variants.note: European Portuguese pronunciation differs; the sentences are otherwise identical in structure, with a slightly different word for 'busy'.

examples.text: Eu moro nesta rua.

translations.de: Ich wohne in dieser Straße.
translations.en: I live on this street.
translations.fr: J'habite dans cette rue.

examples.text: À noite, as ruas ficam vazias.

translations.de: Nachts sind die Straßen leer.
translations.en: The streets are empty at night.
translations.fr: La nuit, les rues sont vides.

more.definition: street; road (paved path); streets (urban areas outside buildings)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese rua (“street”), from or influenced by Old French rue (Modern French rue) or Old Spanish rua (Modern Spanish rúa), from Vulgar Latin *ruga (“furrow, path, street”), from Latin ruga (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewp- (“to become encrusted”). Cognate with Galician rúa. Doublet of ruga.

usage_note: Portuguese distinguishes 'rua' (town street) from 'estrada' (road between places).

more.definition: sense (animals’ means of gathering data); sense (natural appreciation or ability); purpose; intention
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentido, past participle of sentir, from Latin sentīre (“to feel”), from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to head for, go”).

more.definition: prison; arrest; captivity
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prison, borrowed from Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiō, from prehendō (“to seize”) + -tiō. Doublet of preensão.

senses.gloss_en: to marry, to get married, to wed

more.definition: to marry; to get married; to marry someone (unite two others in wedlock)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese casar (13th century), probably from casa + -ar.

more.definition: choice (opportunity to choose or select something); the act of choosing
more.etymology: Deverbal from escolher (“to choose”).

more.definition: own; proper, adequate; peculiar, particular
more.etymology: Latin propriuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin proprius (“own”).

more.definition: hair, head of hair; hair (a single hair filament); body hair, especially if long
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabelo (“hair”).

more.definition: amusing; comical; curious, peculiar, weird
more.etymology: Latin grātialbor. From en- + graça (“joke”) + -ado. Compare Spanish gracioso.

more.definition: police officer
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-tósder. Ancient Greek πολῑτείᾱ (polīteíā)bor. Late Latin polītīalbor. From polícia + -al.

more.definition: perfect; perfective
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *per-der. Inherited from Latin perfectus.

more.definition: loud; tall; high
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese alto, from Latin altus, ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. This form is likely a semi-learned term, or was influenced by learned elements of the language and uses such an orthography, as with Galician and Spanish alto (which have popularly inherited variants outo and oto, respectively).

more.definition: free; unoccupied; clear, open
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese livre, libre, from Latin līber, from Old Latin loeber, from Proto-Italic *louðeros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-er-os, from *h₁lewdʰ- (“people”).

more.definition: safe; secure (free from danger); sure; certain (without doubt); self-confident (confident in one’s abilities)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese seguro, from Latin sēcūrus (“careless”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish seguro, Catalan and Occitan segur, French sûr, Italian sicuro and English sicker.

more.definition: girl (female child); young lady, miss (a title of respect for an unmarried young woman); an effeminate boy
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese meninha, from meninho.

regional_variants.note: Portugal contracts em + uma to numa in writing too.

examples.text: Que dia bonito!

translations.de: Was für ein schöner Tag!
translations.en: What a beautiful day!
translations.fr: Quelle belle journée !

examples.text: A cidade é bonita na primavera.

translations.de: Die Stadt ist im Frühling schön.
translations.en: The city is beautiful in spring.
translations.fr: La ville est belle au printemps.

more.definition: pretty, lovely
more.etymology: Spanish bonitobor. Borrowed from Spanish bonito (“pretty, lovely”), from bueno (“good”) + -ito (diminutive suffix).

more.definition: future (the time ahead); future tense
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin futūrus (“about to be”).

more.definition: uncle (brother of someone's father or mother, or an aunt's husband); guy; bloke; an employee who performs a given activity
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tio, from Late Latin thīus, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Galician and Spanish tío, Italian zio, Sardinian tiu.

more.definition: to understand, to grasp, to comprehend; to have a good or satisfactory relationship (with someone)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese entender, from Latin intendere. Doublet of intender, a borrowing.

senses.gloss_en: cop, constable, police constable, police officer

more.definition: agent (one who exerts power)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin agente. By surface analysis, agir + -ente.

more.definition: sign; mark; trace (a visible or otherwise perceivable indication of something); mark (a blemish, stain, scratch, scar or similar on a surface, especially on the skin); signal (a visual or audible indication made to give notice of some occurrence, command or danger)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sinal, synal, from Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum. By surface analysis, sino + -al. Cognate with Spanish señal f, French signal m, and English signal.

more.definition: group (number of things or persons being in some relation to each other); group (people who perform music together); group
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *grewbʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *kruppazder. Frankish *kruppbor. Italian gruppobor. Borrowed from Italian gruppo. Compare Renaissance Latin grupus.

more.definition: to walk (to move on one’s feet); to walk (to travel through a given path); to ride; to take; to travel by (to use a given mode of transportation)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese andar, from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin.

more.definition: the present; present, gift
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese presente, from Latin praesentem.

more.definition: face (part of head)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rosto, rostro, from Latin rōstrum. Doublet of rostro, a learned borrowing.

more.definition: table (item of furniture); meal, food; mesa
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mesa (“table”), from Vulgar Latin mēsa, from Latin mēnsa (“table”). Cognate with Galician mesa, Spanish mesa, French moise, Italian mensa and Romanian masă. Not related to Persian میز (mêz, “table”). As both it and Portuguese mesa have been borrowed into different languages of southern Asia, they are sometimes confused by etymologists.

more.definition: pain (physical or emotional)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese door, from Latin dolōrem (“pain”). Compare Galician dor and Spanish dolor.

more.definition: photo; photograph
more.etymology: French photographiebor. Portuguese fotografiaclip. Clipping of fotografia.

more.definition: light (of low weight; not heavy); gentle, light (having little force)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese leve, from Latin levis, from Proto-Italic *leɣʷis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ- (“light”). Doublet of léu.

more.definition: to split (divide something, especially in two roughly equal parts); to split; to break apart (become divided, especially in two roughly equal parts); to depart; to leave; to go away
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-yétider. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese partir, from Latin partīre.

more.definition: category into which sexually-reproducing organisms are divided on the basis of their reproductive roles in their species; another category, especially for humans and often separable, based on non-physical traits or roles; gender; sexual intercourse
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sek-der. Proto-Indo-European *séks-u-sder. Latin sexuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin sexus.

more.definition: voice (all senses); speech
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *wekʷ-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese voz, from Latin vōcem, from Proto-Italic *wōks, from Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs.

more.definition: killer, murderer, assassin
more.etymology: From Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn, “fundamentalist”).

more.definition: contraction of de (“from”) + aí (“there (near you)”); then, afterwards, thus
situation (one's status with regard to circumstances)
more.etymology: Latin -tiōnemlbor. From situar + -ção.

more.definition: air; look, air (aspect)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aar, from Latin āēr, borrowed from Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ήρ (āḗr, “air”), from Proto-Hellenic *auhḗr, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewsér, from *h₂ews- + *-r.

more.definition: simple; Generally lower-class; uneducated and/or poor.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sm̥-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese simplez, from Latin simplex.

senses.gloss_en: to save, to rescue, to recover, to escape

more.definition: to save (to help someone to survive; to make sure something isn’t destroyed); to save (to write a file to disk); to save (to redeem or protect someone from eternal damnation)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese salvar, from Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus (“safe”), from Proto-Indo-European *solo- (“whole”).

more.definition: to know (be acquainted or familiar with); to meet; to get to know (to become acquainted with); to know (someone/something) (to ascribe to something the title or quality of)
more.etymology: From older conhocer, from Old Galician-Portuguese connocer, from Latin cognōscere.

more.definition: job (economic role for which a person is paid); use; usage (the act of using something or the way something is used); employment (the state of being employed)
more.etymology: Deverbal from empregar (“to employ”).

more.definition: ten
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dez, from Latin decem (“ten”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

more.definition: message (concept or information conveyed); message (underlying theme or conclusion to be drawn from something)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missaticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).

more.definition: age (part of the duration of a being or thing between its beginning and any given time)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ydade, from Latin aetātem, from syncope of earlier aevitās, from Proto-Italic *aiwotāts, from *aiwom + *-tāts, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital energy”), from *h₂ey-.

more.definition: question (phrase asking for information); question (a request for an answer in a test); matter; issue (a point in debate or controversy)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese questam, from Latin quaestiōnem (“inquiry; question”).

more.definition: bring (to transport toward somebody/somewhere)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese trager, from Vulgar Latin tragere, from Latin trahere. Cognate of Spanish traer, French traire, and Italian trarre.

more.definition: premises, rooms; site; place, location
more.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with the inherited lugar.

more.definition: beautiful; gorgeous;
more.etymology: Uncertain. Probably ultimately from Latin legitimus (“lawful; proper”), and likely through the intermediate of Spanish lindo (the native Portuguese descendant (and thus its doublet) in this case is lídimo; there is also the later learned borrowing legítimo).

more.definition: sick (in poor health); weak; sad
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese doente, from Latin dolentem (“hurting, suffering”). Compare Spanish doliente, Italian dolente. Doublet of dolente, a borrowing.

more.definition: natal (of or relating to birth); native (relating to the place where one was born)
more.etymology: Latin nātālislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin nātālis. Doublet of Natal and Noel.

more.definition: teacher (a person who teaches professionally); coach; referee
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂-der. Latin professorlbor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese professor, a learned borrowing from Latin professor, from professus + -tor.

more.definition: motive (that which incites to action); motif (short melodic passage that is repeated in several parts of a work)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-iHwósder. Medieval Latin mōtīvuslbor. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin mōtīvus.

senses.gloss_en: to follow, to pursue, to trace

more.definition: to follow (to go or come after in physical space); to follow (to occur afterwards); to follow (carry out instructions)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese seguir, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre, from deponent Classical Latin sequī, from Proto-Italic *sekʷōr, from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

more.definition: country; countryside; field (large open area, especially one where crops are grown or sports are played); field (domain of knowledge or practice)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese campo, from Latin campus (“wild field”). Doublet of campus, a borrowing from Latin. Compare Galician and Spanish campo.

more.definition: normal, standard, regular; normal (perpendicular to a tangent of a curve or derivative of a surface)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₃sḱétider. Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn)bor. Latin normālislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin normālis. By surface analysis, norma + -al.

more.definition: will; the condition of feeling like or wanting something; desire, wish; intention; purpose
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese voontade, from the Latin voluntās, voluntātis (“will; desire; disposition toward”). Cognate with Galician vontade and Spanish voluntad.

more.definition: boy (a young male)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese meninho (the palatal nasal survives in the Galician cognate meniño), of uncertain origin: * From Latin minimus. * From a Gallo-Romance language (cf. Catalan minyó (“boy”), French mignon (“cute”)). * From meu ninno, with ninno being a borrowing from Old Spanish niño.

more.definition: ground, soil, earth; floor; land
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chão (“ground”), from Latin plānum (“level ground”) < plānus, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Compare Galician chan and Spanish llano. Doublet of plano, porão, piano, and lhano.

more.definition: sun; sunlight, sunshine (the light and heat which are received from the sun); sun (a day); sun (a star, especially one at the center of a solar system)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sol, from Latin sōl (“sun”).

more.definition: surprise (something not expected); surprise (feeling that something unexpected has happened); a present; a gift
more.etymology: Borrowed from French surprise, from Old French surprendre (“to overtake”), from sur- (“over”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin prendere (“to seize”).

more.definition: list
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese lista, from Italian lista, from Old High German līsta, from Proto-Germanic *līstōn.

more.definition: dream (imaginary events seen while sleeping); dream (a deep hope or desire); a traditional Christmas treat prepared with eggs and flour, fried in olive oil; beignet, fritter
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *swep-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sonho, from Latin somnium. Compare Galician soño, Spanish sueño, Italian sogno, and French songe.

examples.text: Ela está com alguma coisa no olho.

translations.de: Sie hat etwas im Auge.
translations.en: She has something in her eye.
translations.fr: Elle a quelque chose dans l'œil.

examples.text: Ele tem olhos azuis.

translations.de: Er hat blaue Augen.
translations.en: He has blue eyes.
translations.fr: Il a les yeux bleus.

more.definition: eye; eye, center (of a storm, etc.); a hole in cheese, bread or similar items
collocations: de olho em — keeping an eye on
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese olho, from Vulgar Latin oclum, from Latin oculum (“eye”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Doublet of óculo, a borrowing. Compare Galician ollo, Spanish ojo, French œil and Italian occhio.

senses.gloss_en: to end, to finish, to complete, to terminate

more.definition: to finish; to complete (to reach the end of an activity); to finish; to end (to be over); to finish
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Latin terminārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin termināre (“to limit; to finish”).

more.definition: answer, response
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese resposta, reposta, from responder, corrupted by posta, feminine past participle of põer (Portuguese pôr). Compare Asturian and Spanish respuesta, Catalan and Galician resposta and Italian risposta.

more.definition: to drink (something); to consume alcoholic beverages; to drink something
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese beber, bever (“to drink”), from Latin bibere (“to drink”), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Galician beber and Spanish beber, Catalan and Occitan beure, French boire, Italian bere and Romanian bea.

more.definition: order (arrangement, disposition); order (the state of being well arranged); order; command
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ordin, orden, from Latin ōrdinem m.

more.definition: hotel
more.etymology: Borrowed from French hôtel, from Latin hospitāle. Doublet of hospital and hospedal.

more.definition: people; hamlet (a small village or a group of houses); mob
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese poboo (displacing collateral form poblo), from Latin populus (“people, nation”), from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”), maybe from Etruscan. Cognate with Galician pobo.

more.definition: accident (unexpected event with negative consequences); accident (irregular surface)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin accidentem, present active participle of accidō (“happen”); from ad (“to”) + cadō (“fall”); respectively from Proto-Indo-European *ád (“near, at”) and *ḱad- (“to fall”).

more.definition: error; mistake; error (failure to complete a task, usually involving a premature termination); error (difference between a measured value and a true one)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese erro, from earlier error, borrowed from Latin errōrem; alternatively, a deverbal from errar (compare Spanish yerro).

more.definition: lawyer (individual trained in Law and legally qualified to exercise judicial mandate and other technical and legal functions as a profession); advocate
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese avogado (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), influenced by Latin advocātus. Compare Spanish abogado and Galician avogado.

more.definition: anniversary; birthday
more.etymology: Proto-Italic *worssosder. Latin anniversāriuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin anniversārius.

more.definition: hell (where sinners go); a very unpleasant or negative situation; a very hot place
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese inferno, iferno, from Latin īnfernus (“infernal; of the lower regions”).

more.definition: attack (an attempt to cause damage, injury to, or death of an opponent or enemy); attack (an attempt to detract from the worth or credibility of someone or something); attack (the sudden onset of a disease or condition)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Middle French destacherbor. Italian attaccarebor. Portuguese atacardeverb. Deverbal from atacar.

more.definition: to open; to deal (a card)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese abrir, from Latin aperīre, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“off, from”) + *wer-iō (“open”).

more.definition: hunger (need or compelling desire for food); hunger (any strong desire); famine (extreme shortage of food in a region)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fame, from Latin famēs (“hunger”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin alternative accusative form Latin *fam(i)ne(m), or more likely a variant nominative form *famen), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”).

more.definition: totally
more.etymology: From total + -mente.

more.definition: shop, store; basement, cellar; lodge (local chapter of freemasons)
more.etymology: Frankish *laubijābor. Early Medieval Latin laubiader. Old French logebor. French logesl. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese logea (“storehouse”). Sense 3 is a semantic loan from French loge.

more.definition: conversation; talking; an instance of conversation; bullshit; nonsense (untrue statements intended to deceive)
more.etymology: Latin conversārelbor. Portuguese conversardeverb. Deverbal from conversar (“to converse”), a learned borrowing from Latin conversāre.

more.definition: interval of time; empty space; set of points
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espaço, from Latin spatium. Cognate with Galician espazo, Spanish espacio.

more.definition: service (work that is produced, traded, sold, then consumed); work; labour; job; a task
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese serviço, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin servitium (“slavery; servitude”) (compare Italian servizio, French service, Norman sèrvice, Spanish servicio), from servus (“serf”). By surface analysis, servo + -iço.

more.definition: mount; a mountain or large hill; pile; heap (a mass of things placed together so as to form a mass or elevation); heap; load; pile (a great amount of something)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese monte m, from Latin montem. Compare Galician monte m.

more.definition: murder (unlawful premeditated killing of one person by another); assassination (murder of an important figure)
more.etymology: From assassino (“assassin”) + -ato, from Italian assassino, from Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”).

more.definition: law
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese lei, ley, from earlier lee, from Latin lēgem, from Proto-Italic *lēg-, from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ-s < *leǵ-. Cognate with Galician lei, Spanish ley, Catalan llei, Occitan lei, French loi, Italian legge and Romanian lege.

more.definition: bank (financial institution); bank (safe place for storage and retrieval of items); bench (long seat)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Italian banco, from Old High German bank, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz.

more.definition: completely; fully; totally (to a complete extent or degree); completely; extremely; utterly (to a very high extent or degree)
more.etymology: From completa + -mente.

more.definition: fun; amusing; entertaining
more.etymology: From divertir (“to amuse; to divert”).

more.definition: deep (having its bottom far down)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fundo, fondo, from Latin fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.

more.definition: bottom; background (a part of the picture that depicts scenery to the rear or behind the main subject); fund
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese fundo, fondo, from Latin fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn.

senses.gloss_en: to fight, to struggle, to wrestle

more.definition: to fight (participate in a conflict); to fight (participate in a conflict against an enemy); to fight, to struggle (try to stop something)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *lewg-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese luitar, from Latin luctārī. Compare Galician loitar, Spanish luchar.

more.definition: to explain
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ-der. Latin explicārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin explicāre.

more.definition: sky; heaven
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ceo (“sky; heaven”), from Latin caelum (“sky”), from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-. Cognate with Galician ceo, Spanish cielo, Catalan cel, Occitan cèl, French ciel, Italian cielo and Romanian cer.

more.definition: army
more.etymology: Latin exercituslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin exercitus.

more.definition: month (each of the twelve periods into which the year is divided); month (period between any date in one month and the corresponding date in the following month); month (period of thirty consecutive days)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mes, from Latin mēnsis. Compare Galician, Spanish, and Catalan mes, Italian mese, French mois, and Romansh mais.

more.definition: letter (written message); chart, map (visual representation of an area); playing card (any of the 52 rectangular pieces of card used to play games)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese carta, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”). Doublet of cartaz.

regional_variants.note: Portugal puts the pronoun after the verb: lembro-me.

examples.text: Eu me lembro do meu primeiro dia de aula.

translations.de: Ich erinnere mich an meinen ersten Schultag.
translations.en: I remember my first day of school.
translations.fr: Je me souviens de mon premier jour d'école.

examples.text: Você se lembra do nome dela?

translations.de: Erinnerst du dich an ihren Namen?
translations.en: Do you remember her name?
translations.fr: Tu te souviens de son nom ?

more.definition: to remember; to remind; to resemble; to remind one of (to look similar)
collocations: se bem me lembro — if I remember correctly
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese nembrar, from Latin memorāre. Doublet of memorar (a borrowing).

more.definition: contact; touch; connection
more.etymology: Latin contāctuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin contāctus.

more.definition: paper (sheet material typically used for writing on or printing); (written) document; paper (an open hand in rock paper scissors)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese papel, borrowed from Old Catalan paper, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin papȳrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros). Doublet of pavio and papiro.

more.definition: government
more.etymology: Ancient Greek κυβερνάω (kubernáō)bor. Portuguese governardeverb. Deverbal from governar. Compare Italian governo, Spanish gobierno.

more.definition: entertaining; amusing; worthy of consideration; in one’s interest; unique, strange or unexpected; curious
more.etymology: Spanish interesantebor. Borrowed from Spanish interesante. By surface analysis, interessar (“to interest”) + -ante.

more.definition: cause of horror; horrible; terrible
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin horribilis.

more.definition: certainly
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese certamente. By surface analysis, certa + -mente. Compare Galician certamente.

more.definition: flat, apartment
more.etymology: Borrowed from Italian appartamento, possibly through French appartement and/or Spanish apartamento. Ultimately from Spanish apartamiento (“separation, seclusion”), from apartar (“to separate”). By surface analysis, apartar + -mento.

more.definition: half (one of two equal parts into which anything may be divided); middle; midpoint (point equidistant between two extremes); middle (time between the beginning and the end)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese metade displacing collateral form meiadade, from Late Latin medietātem (“center; midpoint”), from Latin medius (“middle; half”), from Proto-Indo-European *medʰyo- (“between”). Compare Spanish mitad.

senses.gloss_en: to search, to seek, to look for

more.definition: to search; to seek; to look for; to reach out (attempt to initiate communication); to try; to attempt
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese procurar, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, to administer”), from Latin prāre + cūrō (“to take care; to cure; to manage”). Cognate of English procure.

more.definition: sad; unhappy; down; sad (causing sadness); disappointed
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese triste, presumably a borrowing from Latin trīstis.

more.definition: examination; test; proof; evidence (fact or observation presented in support of an assertion); evidence (anything admitted by a court to prove or disprove alleged matters of fact in a trial)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese prova, either regressively derived from the verb provar or from Late Latin proba (“proof”), from Latin probō (“to approve; to prove”), from probus (“good”).

more.definition: boat (water craft)
more.etymology: Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare)der. Ancient Greek βᾶρῐς (bârĭs)der. Vulgar Latin -icusder. From barca (“barge”), from Old Galician-Portuguese barca, from Late Latin barca, syncope of Vulgar Latin *bārica, from Latin bāris + Vulgar Latin -ica.

more.definition: decision
more.etymology: From decidir + -são, or borrowed from Latin dēcīsiōnem.

more.definition: lieutenant (a low commissioned officer rank)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin tenentem. By surface analysis, ter + -ente.

more.definition: advice; council
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese conselho, from Latin cōnsilium. Doublet of consílio, a borrowing. Compare Galician consello.

more.definition: airplane, aeroplane (heavier-than-air aircraft); attractive or well-endowed woman
more.etymology: Borrowed from French avion (“airplane”), coined by Clément Ader after Latin avis (“bird”), equivalent to ave + -ão.

more.definition: to read (to look at and interpret written information); to read (to speak aloud written information); to read (to fetch data from)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese leer, from Latin lēgere. Compare Galician ler and Spanish leer.

more.definition: to touch, to finger, to feel (tactually); to start addressing; to play (a musical instrument)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.

more.definition: brief, short; summarized; minute (very small)
more.etymology: Probably a borrowing from Latin brevis (“short”) (compare Spanish breve, where *brieve would be expected if the term were inherited), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus.

more.definition: having low temperatures; cool; insensitive
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese frio, from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frigus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sriHgos-, *sriges-, *sriHges-. Compare Galician and Spanish frío, Asturian fríu, Catalan fred, Italian freddo. Doublet of frígido.

more.definition: pub; bar (establishment that serves alcoholic beverages primarily); bar (unit of pressure)
more.etymology: Borrowed from English bar. Doublet of barra.

more.definition: key (object that opens and closes a lock); key (object that is inserted into a device and rotated to activate it); any of several tools designed to turn screws, bolts, nuts, etc., especially a spanner
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese chave (“key”), from Latin clāvis (“key”), from Proto-Italic *klāwis (“bolt, lock, bar”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂w- (“nail, pin, hook - instruments, of old use for locking doors”) (possibly through an Ancient Greek intermediate). Doublet of clave, a learned borrowing.

more.definition: impossible (not able to be done); impossible (very difficult to deal with); unbearable
more.etymology: Latin impossibilisslbor. Semi-learned borrowing from Latin impossibilis. By surface analysis, im- + possível.

more.definition: church (a house of worship); a Christian denomination
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese igreja, from Latin ecclēsia (“church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “congregation”). Cognate with Galician igrexa, Spanish iglesia Catalan església, Occitan glèisa, French église, and Italian chiesa. Doublet of eclésia, a borrowing.

more.definition: boyfriend (a male lover); Namorado sandperch (Pseudopercis numida)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese namorado, from namorar, from en- + amor (“love”) + -ar. Compare Catalan enamorat, Spanish enamorado and Italian innamorato.

more.definition: terrible
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin terribilis. By surface analysis, terror + -ível.

more.definition: wonderful
more.etymology: From maravilha + -oso. Compare Spanish maravilloso.

senses.gloss_en: to there is, to exist, to be around

more.definition: there be; exist; there be; to happen; to occur; ago (indicates the time since something occurred)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aver, from Latin habēre. Compare Galician haber. Cognate of Spanish haber, French avoir, and Italian avere.

more.definition: secret
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin sēcrētum. Doublet of secreto.

more.definition: truthful (accurately depicting what is real); true; loyal; faithful; genuine; legitimate
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese verdadeiro. By surface analysis, verdade + -eiro. Compare Spanish verdadero.

more.definition: seven
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sete, from Latin septem, from Proto-Italic *septəm, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.

more.definition: victim
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *weyk-der. Latin victimalbor. Learned borrowing from Latin victima (“sacrificial victim”).

more.definition: ship; nave, aisle; car
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nave, from Latin nāvis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Doublet of nau.

more.definition: immediately
more.etymology: From imediata + -mente.

more.definition: to fall; to fall down; to drop; to fall (to fall so it is no longer attached to or on top of something); to fall; to collapse (to be overthrown, defeated or annulled)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caer, from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre, from Proto-Italic *kadō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱad- (“to fall”). Cognate with Galician caer and Spanish caer.
From Old Galician-Portuguese tu, from Latin tū (“you”), from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂ (“you”).

more.definition: gold (chemical element); gold (coin); gold (colour)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ouro, from Latin aurum, from Latin ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- (“glow”).

more.definition: poor
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pobre, poubre, from Latin pauperem, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”).

more.definition: soul
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese alma, from Latin anima (“soul, breath”). Doublet of anima, borrowed from the same source.

more.definition: general (highest rank in the category of Army and Air Force officers, whose insignia consists of four stars); chief, leader; general (officer holding that post)
more.etymology: Latin generālislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin generālis. Doublet of geral.

more.definition: master; mentor; master (person holding a master's degree)
more.etymology: Old Occitan maestrebor. Old Catalan maestrebor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese meestre, from earlier maestre, via Old Occitan maestre or Old Catalan maestre, from Latin magistrum. Alternatively inherited from the Latin nominative magister. Cognate with Galician mestre. Doublet of maestro, magíster, máster, and míster.

examples.text: Esqueci meu celular em casa.

translations.de: Ich habe mein Handy zu Hause vergessen.
translations.en: I forgot my cell phone at home.
translations.fr: J'ai oublié mon portable à la maison.

examples.text: Os celulares devem ficar desligados.

translations.de: Handys müssen ausgeschaltet sein.
translations.en: Cell phones must be turned off.
translations.fr: Les portables doivent être éteints.

more.definition: cell phone; smartphone
collocations: número de celular — cell phone number
more.etymology: Ellipsis of telefone celular.

more.definition: horse (Equus ferus caballus); knight; heroin
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cavalo, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), from Gaulish *kaballos, from Proto-Celtic *kaballos, perhaps ultimately an Asiatic borrowing or Wanderwort, compare Ancient Greek καβάλλης (kabállēs, “nag”), Proto-Slavic *kobýla (“mare”), Persian کول (kaval, “second class horse of mixed blood”), and possibly Karakhanid [script needed] (kevel (at), …

more.definition: company, companionship; companion; company
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese companhia. Cognate with Galician and Spanish compañía, Catalan companyia, French compagnie, Italian compagnia, Occitan companhiá and English company.

more.definition: just, only, merely
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese soomente~soamente, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. By surface analysis, só + -mente.

more.definition: to forget
more.etymology: From earlier esqueecer, from Old Galician-Portuguese escaecer, from Vulgar Latin *excadescere, derived ultimately from Latin cadere (“fall”). Compare Galician esquecer.

more.definition: to seem; to resemble
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parecer, from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.

more.definition: beginning; commencement (the process of beginning, starting); beginning; start (the initial stages of something)
more.etymology: Deverbal from começar.

more.definition: bad; evil, wicked; harmful
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mao, from Latin malus, from Proto-Italic. Cognate with Galician mao and Spanish malo.

regional_variants.note: European Portuguese prefers 'aldeia' for a small village; 'vilarejo' is more Brazilian.

examples.text: A estrada para o vilarejo é muito estreita.

translations.de: Die Straße zum Dorf ist sehr schmal.
translations.en: The road to the village is very narrow.
translations.fr: La route du village est très étroite.

examples.text: Muitas estradas estão fechadas por causa da neve.

translations.de: Viele Straßen sind wegen des Schnees gesperrt.
translations.en: Many roads are closed because of the snow.
translations.fr: Beaucoup de routes sont fermées à cause de la neige.

more.definition: road
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese estrada, strada, from Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus.

usage_note: For a street in a town, Portuguese uses 'rua'; 'estrada' is for roads between places.

more.definition: dress (woman’s garment which covers the upper part of the body as well as below the waist); garment (single item of clothing)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese vestido, from Latin vestītus (“dressed; clothing”), perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to dress”), from vestis (“clothes”).

more.definition: position (place, location); posture (way a person holds and positions their body); position (place assigned to a player)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin positiōnem. By surface analysis, pôr + -ção.

more.definition: full, filled, completed; covered; full (of people), crowded (having a large number of people)
more.etymology: Proto-Italic *plēnosder. Earlier cheo. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chẽo, from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Doublet of pleno, a learned borrowing. Related to words such as Galician cheo, Spanish lleno, Catalan ple, and, more distantly, English full.

more.definition: link; connection; bond (link or force between neighbouring atoms in a molecule)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin ligātiōnem. By surface analysis, ligar + -ção. Compare Galician and Spanish ligazón, French liaison.

more.definition: together (at the same time, in the same place); near, next
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese junto, from Latin iūnctus.

more.definition: planet
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese planeta f or m, from Latin planēta, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs) variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin.

more.definition: hard (resistant to pressure; not soft); hard (difficult; not easy); unrelenting, unfriendly, severe, brutal, harsh
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese duro, from Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”).

more.definition: step; footstep; pace (movement made from one foot to the other); Portuguese pace, a former unit of length equivalent to about 1.6 m; step (very short distance)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese passo, from Latin passus. Cognate with Catalan pas and Galician and Spanish paso.

more.definition: yours (singular) (that or those belonging to, associated with, related to, or in the possession of you)
more.etymology: Proto-Italic *towosder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tou, from Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.

senses.gloss_en: to safeguard, to protect, to put on a safety catch

more.definition: to protect; to support
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin protegere.

more.definition: long
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese longo, from Latin longus, from Proto-Indo-European *dl̥h₁gʰós (“long”).

more.definition: puppy (a young dog); dog (of any age); a promiscuous man
more.etymology: Uncertain. Likely inherited from Vulgar Latin *cattulus, from Latin catulus, plus the suffix -orro; whence also Spanish cachorro. Compare with Italian cucciolo.

more.definition: to write (to form letters, etc.)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese escrever, escrivir, from Latin scrībere (“to write”), from Proto-Italic *skreiβō, from Proto-Indo-European *skreybʰ- (“to write”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish escribir, Catalan and Occitan escriure, French écrire, Italian scrivere, Romanian scrie and English shrive.

more.definition: equal
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese igual, ygual, from Latin aequālis.

more.definition: to order, command; to tell to do something (may or may not have a commanding tone); to order, to boss around
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mandar, from Latin mandāre (“to order, to commission”).

senses.gloss_en: to beat, to hit, to knock, to ring someone's bell

more.definition: to beat; to beat up (to attack someone violently); to hit; to strike (to collide with violently); to crash (to cause something to collide)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bater, from Latin battere, from earlier battuere. Compare Galician bater.

more.definition: back (the rear of body); backstroke
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese costas (“back”), from Latin costa (“rib”).

senses.gloss_en: to taste, to get a taste of

more.definition: to prove, show, to demonstrate that something is true, to give proof for; to try, try out, test; to try, attempt, take on
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese provar, from Latin probāre.

more.definition: both
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ambos, from Latin ambōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“round about, around”).

more.definition: to learn, to acquire knowledge; to be able to learn
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aprender, from Latin apprendere, alternative form of apprehendere. Doublet of apreender, a borrowing. Compare Galician aprender.

senses.gloss_en: to run, to race, to sprint

more.definition: to run (to move quickly on one’s feet); to run away; to flee; to speed (to drive too fast)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese correr, from Latin currere (“to run”), from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”).

more.definition: company; business; enterprise
more.etymology: Italian imprenderedeverb. Italian impresabor. Borrowed from Italian impresa.

more.definition: information
more.etymology: Latin īnfōrmātiōnemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem. By surface analysis, informar + -ção.

more.definition: danger (exposure to liable harm); danger (an instance or cause of liable harm)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perigoo, probably a semi-learned word from Latin perīculum (“danger”). Compare Galician perigo and Spanish peligro.

more.definition: relation, connection, association; involvement between people, affective or not; sexual relation
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin relātiōnem (“a bringing back, restoring”), from relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“carry back; report”).

more.definition: sweet, sugary; fresh; gentle, sweet, kind
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese doce, from Latin dulcem (“sweet”). Doublet of Dulce. Compare Galician doce and Sicilian duci.

more.definition: destiny, fate; destination
more.etymology: Latin dēstinārelbor. Portuguese destinardeverb. Deverbal from destinar.

more.definition: white (color); white; Caucasian; pale; pallid
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *bʰleyǵ-der. Frankish *blankbor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese branco, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, borrowed from Frankish *blank. Cognate with Galician branco, Spanish blanco. Doublet of Blanco and Bianca.

examples.text: Eu gosto dessa música.

translations.de: Ich mag dieses Lied.
translations.en: I like this song.
translations.fr: J'aime cette chanson.

examples.text: Ela gosta de ler à noite.

translations.de: Sie liest abends gern.
translations.en: She likes to read in the evening.
translations.fr: Elle aime lire le soir.

more.definition: to like
collocations: gostar muito de — to like a lot
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese gostar, from Latin gustāre. Compare Spanish gustar.

more.definition: beer
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cerveja, from Latin cervēs(i)a. Compare Spanish cerveza.

more.definition: to solve; to resolve (to find an answer or solution); to decide; to dissolve; to dissipate
more.etymology: From Latin resolvere (“to release”), from re- (“again”) + solvō (“to loosen, to unbind”).

more.definition: to seat; to sit; to place (to put (an object or person) in a specific location)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sentar, from Vulgar Latin *sedentare, from Latin sedeō + *-entāre.

more.definition: the act of shooting; a fired shot; shooting firearms as a sport
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *der-der. Portuguese tirardeverb. Deverbal from tirar (“to remove”).

more.definition: aunt (sister of someone's father or mother, or an uncle's wife); aunt (colloquial term of address for an older woman); colloquial term of address for any female person
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂der. Ancient Greek θείᾱ (theíā)bor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tia, from Late Latin thīa, borrowed from Ancient Greek θείᾱ (theíā, “aunt”).

more.definition: intelligent (of high or especially quick cognitive capacity, bright)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin intelligentem, form of intellegēns (“understanding”).

more.definition: tea plant (Camellia sinensis, a bush whose leaves are used to make tea); tea (drink made by infusing parts of plants); a late afternoon meal
more.etymology: Borrowed from Cantonese 茶 (caa4, “tea”). Portuguese-language dictionaries state Mandarin as the source language, but the historical Portuguese tea trade was centered around Cantonese-speaking regions of China.

more.definition: human (of or belonging to the species Homo sapiens); humane
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese humano, umano (displacing collateral form humão), from Latin hūmānus. Cognate with Galician and Spanish humano, Catalan humà, Occitan and Romanian uman, French humain, Italian umano.

more.definition: in a straight line; direct, without interruption; straight, truthful, frank, sincere
more.etymology: Modified from learned form directo, borrowed from Latin dīrēctus (“straight”), from dīrigō (“lay straight; direct; distribute”), from dis- + regō (“to rule, to govern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-. Compare the inherited direito.

more.definition: to sing (express sounds musically through the voice); to sing, to say musically; to say with rhythm, chant
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cantar, from Latin cantāre.

examples.text: O trem parte às oito.

translations.de: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab.
translations.en: The train leaves at eight.
translations.fr: Le train part à huit heures.

examples.text: Os trens costumam atrasar no inverno.

translations.de: Im Winter haben die Züge oft Verspätung.
translations.en: The trains are often late in winter.
translations.fr: Les trains sont souvent en retard en hiver.

more.definition: set (a series of, a group of); train; train (line of connected cars or carriages)
collocations: pegar o trem — to catch the train
more.etymology: Borrowed from English train, from Middle English, from Old French train (“a delay, a drawing out”).

more.definition: direction, way; driving (action of operating a motor vehicle); steering (something used to steer)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Latin dīrēctiōnemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctiōnem.

more.definition: risky, unsafe, dangerous
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese perigooso, from perigo + -oso, or a semi-learned term from Latin perīculōsus. Doublet of periculoso.

more.definition: to confide, entrust; to rely on, trust
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese confiar, from Vulgar Latin *cōnfīdāre, from cōnfīdere.

more.definition: stupid; rude; overused, exaggerated
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. From Latin stupidus.

more.definition: free from sin and guilt; righteous; morally justified; righteous; fair, just
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese justo, from Latin iūstus (“just, righteous”), jūstus, from Proto-Italic *jowestos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.

more.definition: window; a gap left by a milk tooth; window (period of time)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese janella, from Vulgar Latin *iānuella, diminutive of Latin iānua (“door”). Etymology 1, noun sense 3 and etymology 1, noun sense 4 are semantic loans from English window. Compare Galician xanela, Mirandese jinela. Related to Mozarabic יאנה (yʔnh).

more.definition: desire; wish; food craving
more.etymology: Latin dēsīderiuminflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese desejo, from Early Medieval Latin dēsideus (“desire”), from Latin dēsidia (“sloth, debauchery”). Compare Galician desexo, Asturian deséu, Spanish deseo, Aragonese deseyo, Sicilian disiju.

senses.gloss_en: to receive, to adopt, to accept

more.definition: to accept; to receive
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese aceitar, from Latin acceptāre. The short past participle is directly from accipere, the source of acceptāre.

more.definition: wine
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vinho, from Latin vīnum (compare Galician viño, Spanish and Italian vino, Catalan vi, French and Romanian vin, and English wine), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.

more.definition: to dance; to fail, be unsuccessful; to oscillate (particularly fire)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dançar, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre.

more.definition: queen (a monarch or the wife of a king); queen
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese reinha, rainha, from Latin rēgīna. Compare Galician raíña.

more.definition: common; frequent (occurring often or existing in many places); common; mutual (shared by more than one); common; usual; ordinary; run-of-the-mill (having no special characteristics)
more.etymology: From Latin commūnis (“common, public, general”) from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom-moyn-is (“held in common”).

more.definition: court; tribunal
more.etymology: Derived from Latin tribūnal.

more.definition: to sell
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-redup. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vender, from Latin vēndere (“to sell”).

more.definition: beautiful; attractive (having beauty)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese bel, from Latin bellus, from Proto-Indo-European *dw-ene-, adverbial form of *deu- (“to do, perform, revere, show favor”).

more.definition: mechanical or electrical device; ellipsis of máquina de lavar (“washing machine”); person or organisation that seemingly acts like a machine, being particularly efficient, single-minded, or unemotional
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin machina (“a machine, engine, contrivance, device, stratagem, trick”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná), Doric spelling of μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “a machine, engine, contrivance, device”), from μῆχος (mêkhos, “means”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂gh- (“to be able to, to help; power, sorcerer”).

senses.gloss_en: to get, to receive, to be given
to get, to obtain, to receive, to achieve

more.definition: to get; to receive; to collect or receive payment; to receive (to act as a host for guests)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese receber, from Latin recipere (“to receive; to take back”), from re- + capiō (“to take”).

more.definition: lie (intentionally untrue statement)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mentira, from mentir (“to lie”), from Latin mentīrī, denominal verb from mēns (“mind”), in which the meaning "to lie" stems from a semantic shift "to be inventive, have second thoughts" > "to lie, conjure up", from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”), from *men- (“to think”) + *-tis.

more.definition: example (all senses); role model (a person who serves as an example, or whose behavior is emulated by others)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese exemplo, eixemplo, borrowed from Latin exemplum.

more.definition: anger (a strong feeling of displeasure, hostility or antagonism towards someone or something); rabies (viral disease)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese raiva, from earlier ravia, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs. Compare Galician and Spanish rabia.

more.definition: succour; help (aid or assistance given to one in distress)
more.etymology: Latin succurrerelbor. Portuguese socorrerdeverb. Deverbal from socorrer.

more.definition: indirect object of eles and elas; indirect object of vocês, os senhores, and as senhoras
more.etymology: From Latin illis, dative plural of ille. Compare Galician lles, Spanish les.

senses.gloss_en: to choose, to select, to adopt

more.definition: to choose
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escolher, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *excolligere, from Latin ex- + colligere (“to gather”). Compare Galician escoller, Spanish escoger, Catalan escollir.

more.definition: to concern, worry (to cause concern to, cause unrest); to absorb completely, make apprehensive; to worry
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Latin praeoccupārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin praeoccupāre. By surface analysis, pré- + ocupar.

more.definition: wow (exclamation of amazement)
more.etymology: Borrowed from English wow.

more.definition: to throw; to fire (shoot a gun)
more.etymology: From a- + tiro + -ar.

more.definition: never
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese jamais, from Old Occitan ja mais, from Latin iam magis. Cognate with Galician xamais, Spanish jamás, Occitan jamai, French jamais and Italian giammai.

more.definition: red (having red as its color); red (socialist or communist)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vermelho (“red”), from Vulgar Latin *vermiclus, from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”), from vermis (“worm”), ultimately in reference to a scale insect of species Kermes vermilio, used to make a crimson dye. Cognate with Galician vermello, Spanish bermejo, Asturian bermeyu, Catalan vermell, Occitan vermelh, French vermeil and Italian vermiglio. Also related to English vermilion.

more.definition: except, other than
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin exceptus, from excipiō.

more.definition: card (flat, normally rectangular piece of stiff paper or plastic); cardboard (stiff or heavy paper)
more.etymology: From carta + -ão.

more.definition: patient (person receiving medical treatment); patient (noun phrase semantically on the receiving end of an action)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin patientem (“enduring; patient”).

more.definition: hope; katydid (any insect in the family Tettigoniidae)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asperança, from Latin spērāns, from spērō, from Old Latin *spēsō, from spēs (“hope”) + -ō (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, esperar + -ança. Compare Spanish esperanza, French espérance, Italian speranza.
Variant of câmara tracing back to Latin camera; compare English camera. Some sources state that the word may be a Brazilianism.

more.definition: news (a single news item); message; communication
more.etymology: Latin nōtitialbor. Learned borrowing from Latin nōtitia.

more.definition: slowly (at a slow speed)
more.etymology: From de- + vagar.

more.definition: purse, handbag, bag; stock exchange (building and the associated organization); grant, scholarship
more.etymology: Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa)der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese bolssa, from Late Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa). Doublet of bursa.

more.definition: price (cost required to gain possession of something); price (cost of an action or deed)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese preço, prez, from Latin pretium (“price”), from Proto-Indo-European *preti- (“back”).

more.definition: to hide
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese asconder, from Latin abscondere. Doublet of absconder, a borrowing.

more.definition: dog; the Devil; hammer
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese can, from Latin canem. Compare Galician and Spanish can.

more.definition: partner, sidekick; partner (a spouse or other person with whom one shares a domestic, romantic or sexual bond); fellow, pal
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-yétider. Latin -āriusnom. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parceiro, from Latin partiārius.

more.definition: skin (outer protective layer of the body of a person or animal); skin (outer protective layer of fruit); fur
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pele, from Latin pellem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

more.definition: opinion (subjective thought)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese opynion, borrowed from Latin opīniōnem.

more.definition: computer (programmable electronic device)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin computātōrem. Piecewise doublet of contador. By surface analysis, computar + -dor.

examples.text: O ônibus chega em cinco minutos.

translations.de: Der Bus kommt in fünf Minuten.
translations.en: The bus arrives in five minutes.
translations.fr: Le bus arrive dans cinq minutes.

examples.text: Dois ônibus vão para o aeroporto.

translations.de: Zwei Busse fahren zum Flughafen.
translations.en: Two buses go to the airport.
translations.fr: Deux bus vont à l'aéroport.

more.definition: bus (motor vehicle for transporting large numbers of people); horse bus
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin omnibus (“for everyone”), dative plural of omnis (“all”). Doublet of omnibus.

more.definition: pardon; forgiveness
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese perdon, from perdõar (“to forgive”) (Modern Portuguese perdoar).

more.definition: justice; court
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese justiça, borrowed from Latin iūstitia (“justice”). Cognate with Galician xustiza, Spanish justicia, Catalan justícia, Occitan justícia, French justice, Italian giustizia, Sicilian justizzia and Romanian justiție. See also justeza, possibly a doublet.

more.definition: arm (upper limb); upper arm; brachium (part of the arm between the elbow and shoulder); any limb or tentacle
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese braço, from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn, “arm”), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”), from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“short, brief”). Compare Galician brazo, Spanish brazo, Catalan braç, Romanian braț, and Italian braccio.

senses.gloss_en: to create, to shape, to make

more.definition: to create, to put into existence; to invent; to raise (a child)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese criar, from Latin creāre. False friend to Spanish criar.
