more.definition: to steal (to take illegally or without permission); to rob (to steal objects from a location); to cheat (to violate rules in order to gain advantage from a situation)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roubar, from Late Latin raubāre, from Proto-Germanic *raubōną.

more.definition: spirit (the soul of a person or other living being); ghost; nature; characteristic
more.etymology: Latin spīrituslbor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese espirito, a learned borrowing from Latin spīritus. Cognate with Galician espírito and Spanish espíritu.

more.definition: sleepy, tired; fed up, irritated, annoyed, frustrated, disappointed
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese canssado, past participle of canssar (modern Portuguese cansar).

more.definition: ass, butt; asshole
more.etymology: Kimbundu mbundabor. Borrowed from Kimbundu mbunda.

more.definition: especially, particularly
more.etymology: Latin speciālislbor. From especial + -mente.

more.definition: enormous
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₃sḱétider. Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn)bor. Latin ēnōrmislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin ēnōrmis.

senses.gloss_en: to function, to work, to operate, to perform

more.definition: to work; to function
more.etymology: Borrowed from French fonctionner (“to function; to work”), from fonction + -er, from Latin fūnctiōnem (“function”). By surface analysis, função + -ar.

senses.gloss_en: to envision, to envisage, to imagine

more.definition: to imagine (all senses)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin imāginārī, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

more.definition: enemy
more.etymology: From a semi-learned modification of Old Galician-Portuguese ẽemigo, based on its etymology, Latin inimicus, itself from in- (“not”) + amicus (“friend”) (modern amigo).

more.definition: judgment (act of judging); verdict; decision; trial
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdex (“judge”). By surface analysis, julgar + -mento. Compare Spanish juzgamiento, Catalan and Occitan jutjament, French jugement, Italian giudicamento.

more.definition: joke (amusing story); chirping (action of chirping)
more.etymology: From piar.

more.definition: report (information describing events)
more.etymology: From relatar (“to relate, to narrate”) + -ório (“-ory”), from relato (“account; narration”), from Latin relātus (“narration”), past participle of referō (“to carry back; to refer”).

more.definition: to avoid
more.etymology: Latin ēvītārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin ēvītāre.

more.definition: target; goal, objective; object of criticism or ridicule
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Latin albus. Doublet of álbum.

more.definition: piece; moment (of time); hottie (physically or sexually attractive person)
more.etymology: Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion)der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pedaço, from Latin pittacium, from Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion, “receipt, ticket”). Compare Spanish pedazo.

more.definition: to ruin, devastate (proceed with the destruction of, cause the destruction of); to undo; to break down
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese destruir, destroir, from Latin dēstruere (“to destroy”) (probably an early borrowing), from dē + struō (“to put together”).

more.definition: class, kind (group, collection, category or set sharing characteristics or attributes); class; elegance; class (a group of students)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁-der. Latin classislbor. Learned borrowing from Latin classis.

more.definition: to ascend, to go up; to climb; to upload
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese subir, sobir, inherited from Latin subīre (“to approach”).

more.definition: to play, as in child's play or "playing around"; to act with levity or thoughtlessness; to joke, to kid
more.etymology: Probably from brinco (“merriment”) + -ar or less likely from Proto-Germanic *blinkaną (“to gleam, glitter, flash”).

more.definition: pit; hole (hollow spot in a surface); burrow (a tunnel or hole dug by a creature); a very filthy, crude or precarious house
more.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from Old Galician-Portuguese furaco, through Vulgar Latin *foraculum from Latin forāmen (“aperture, opening”). Compare Galician buraco, furaco, furado, Asturian furacu, buracu, Ladino burako, Leonese buraco, Spanish buraco; compare also, just for the card games, Italian burraco and Sicilian vurracu. Cf. also Catalan forat, Spanish horado.

more.definition: gentle; amiable; kind; elegant; gentle; polite; respectful
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese gentil, borrowed from Latin gentīlis (“belonging to the same family”), from gēns (“clan; tribe”).

more.definition: hero (individual who stands out for an act of extraordinary courage, bravery, strength of character, or other quality considered notable); hero (one who is admired for any reason, constituting the center of attention); protagonist
more.etymology: From Latin hērōs (“hero”), from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs, “demi-god, hero”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to watch over, protect”).

more.definition: prison (place of long-term confinement for those convicted of serious crimes); chain (series of interconnected rings or links made of metal); chain (series of interconnected things)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cadea, from Latin catēna, from Proto-Italic *katesnā. Compare Galician cadea, Spanish cadena, and English chain. Doublet of the direct borrowing catena.

more.definition: run (the act of running); race (an attempt to reach some goal before others); a ride on a taxi or other private car
more.etymology: From correr (“to run”), from Old Galician-Portuguese correr, from Latin currō (“to run”).

more.definition: tree
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arvor, from Latin arborem. Compare Galician árbore, Spanish árbol.

more.definition: beginning (initial portion of some extended thing)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineō (“go in, make a start”), from in (“in, into”) + eō (“go”).

more.definition: edifice (a building, especially an imposing one); a large, multi-story building with rooms or floor belonging to different people or used for different purposes, such as an apartment block or skyscraper
more.etymology: Latin -iusnom. Latin praediumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin praedium (“estate”).

more.definition: nervous (easily agitated); nervous; anxious; nervous (relating to the nerves)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin nervōsus (“sinewy; nervous”), corresponding to nervo + -oso.

more.definition: wall (of a house or building)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese parede, from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m. Compare Galician parede, Spanish pared.

more.definition: game, play; frolic, fun; joke; banter
more.etymology: From brincar (“to play”) + -deira.

more.definition: to love, to have great affection for; to have the ability to love, to feel love
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₃emh₃-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese amar, from Latin amāre (“to love”).

more.definition: to cut (to split using a sharp instrument); to cut (to trim or fashion nails, hair, grass, or something similar); to fell; to cut down; to chop down (to drop a tree by cutting its trunk)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(s)kr̥tósder. Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cortar, from Latin curtāre (“to shorten”).

examples.text: Qual é a sua cor favorita?

translations.de: Welche Farbe magst du am liebsten?
translations.en: What is your favorite color?
translations.fr: Quelle est ta couleur préférée ?

examples.text: As folhas de outono têm cores lindas.

translations.de: Herbstblätter haben schöne Farben.
translations.en: Fall leaves have beautiful colors.
translations.fr: Les feuilles d'automne ont de belles couleurs.

more.definition: colour (UK), color (US); complexion; heart
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese coor f, from Latin colōrem m, from Old Latin colos (“covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, conceal”). Doublet of color. Compare Galician cor and Spanish color.

usage_note: "De cor" (by heart) is a different word, said with an open o.

more.definition: ship (large water vessel)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese navio, from Latin nāvigium (“vessel; boat”), from nāvis (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Compare Galician and Spanish navío.

more.definition: clean (not dirty); clean (not having used drugs or alcohol)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese limpo, limpio, from Latin limpidus. Compare límpido, a borrowed doublet.

more.definition: to answer; to reply (to give a written or spoken response); to retort frequently; to correspond to (to be equivalent to)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese responder, from Latin respondēre (“answer”) (likely via Late Latin respondere), from re- & spondeō (“promise”).

more.definition: movement (physical motion); the flow of people or vehicles in a location; movement (group of people with a common ideology who try together to achieve certain general goals)
more.etymology: From mover + -imento, perhaps based partly on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō, from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”).

more.definition: newspaper; news; a day's pay
more.etymology: Borrowed from French journal, from Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”). Doublet of diurno.

more.definition: stone (as a material); stone, rock; rock (closed hand in rock paper scissors)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pedra, from Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra). Cognate with Fala and Galician pedra.

more.definition: animal (any member of the kingdom Animalia); animal (an animal other than a human, especially a vertebrate); twat; idiot; moron
more.etymology: Latin animālisnom. Latin animallbor. Learned borrowing from Latin animal. Doublet of alimária.

more.definition: fish (cold-blooded vertebrate animal that lives in water, moving with the help of fins and breathing with gills)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese peixe, inherited from Latin piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-. Compare Galician peixe.

more.definition: memory (all senses); memoir, dissertation
more.etymology: Latin memorialbor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese memoria, a learned borrowing from Latin memoria.

more.definition: absolutely; completely; entirely; totally; utterly; wholly (in absolute manner)
more.etymology: Latin abder. Proto-Indo-European *s(w)éder. Latin absolvōder. Latin absolūtuslbor. From absoluto + -mente.

more.definition: forest (dense collection of trees)
more.etymology: Ultimately from Early Medieval Latin foresta. Influenced by flor (“flower”).

more.definition: complete; entire (to the greatest extent); total (relating to the whole of something)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis (“total”), from Latin tōtus (“whole”) + -ālis (“-al”).

more.definition: major (military rank); A term of address for someone; brown-chested martin (Progne tapera)
more.etymology: Spanish mayorder. French majorbor. Borrowed from French major. Doublet of maior and mor.

more.definition: neck (part of body)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pescoço, from Old Spanish pescoço (Modern Spanish pescuezo), from *poscoço, from Latin post + Old Spanish coço.

more.definition: to prepare, to get ready (to make ready for a specific future purpose); to cook, to prepare; to plan
more.etymology: Latin praeparārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin praeparāre (“to prepare”).

senses.gloss_en: to confront, to face, to turn oneself in

more.definition: to deliver (to transport something to a destination); to deliver; to hand over; to surrender (to relinquish control or possession of); to reveal (to show non-obvious information)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese entregar, probably a semi-learned term taken from Latin integrāre. Doublet of integrar and inteirar.

more.definition: devil; demon; fiend (creature from Hell); used to emphasise the extent of an action, usually one of a negative nature; evil or perverse person
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese diaboo, displacing the collateral forms diabre, diabro and diablo, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (“devil”) (probably borrowed as a semi-learned term), itself from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “slanderer”). Doublet of diabolô and diábolo.

more.definition: soldier (member of an army); soldier; warrior (person who fights for a cause)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese soldado, corresponding to soldo (“military salary”) + -ado. A calque or imitation of Italian soldato, from the past participle of soldare, from soldo (“money, military pay”). Compare Spanish soldado, Italian soldato, French soldat.

senses.gloss_en: to put, to add, to pour
to place, to put, to stand

more.definition: to put; to place; to get (to position oneself into a given state); to go
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese põer (“to put”), from Latin pōnere, from Proto-Italic *pozinō. Cognate of Spanish poner, French pondre, Italian porre, Sicilian pùniri.

more.definition: strip (long, thin piece of a bigger item); comic strip (a series of drawings); cop; police officer
more.etymology: From tirar (“to remove”), from Old Galician-Portuguese tirar, of uncertain origin.

more.definition: to assist (to help, especially in a secondary role); to watch; to witness; to attend; or also to assist (to help, especially in a secondary role)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin assistere, with change of conjugation.

more.definition: to thank; to be grateful for
more.etymology: Latin -ēscereder. From a- + grado + -ecer.

more.definition: to turn (to change direction); to turn around (to reverse direction); to capsize
more.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *virāre, either from Latin gȳrāre (making it a doublet of girar) or from Latin vibrāre (making it a doublet of vibrar). Compare Catalan virar, French virer and Italian virare.

more.definition: leg (limb); leg (rod-like protrusion from an inanimate object); leg (part of garment)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perna, from Latin perna, from Proto-Indo-European *tpḗrsneh₂ (“heel”). Compare Galician perna and Spanish pierna.

more.definition: visit; visitor
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Portuguese visitardeverb. Deverbal from visitar.

more.definition: image; picture; figure (optical representation of an object); image (mental representation of something seen or imagined); image (outward appearance)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ymagen, omagen, omage, from Latin imāginem (“a copy, likeness, image”), from *im-, also the root of imitor (“to copy, imitate”).

more.definition: to escape (get free)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese escapar, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

senses.gloss_en: to show, to present, to indicate, to demonstrate

more.definition: to introduce (to make multiple people become acquainted with one another); to introduce; to present (to make (someone) become acquainted to); to introduce oneself
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese apresentar, presentar, from Latin praesentāre.

more.definition: distance (space between two points, two places or two objects); timelapse between two moments; interval; separation; remoteness
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Latin distantialbor. Learned borrowing from Latin distantia. By surface analysis, distar + -ância.

more.definition: to cry; to weep (to shed tears from the eyes); to cry (to shed a given substance, or number of tears, from the eyes); to exude; to seep; to ooze
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chorar, from Latin plōrāre (“to lament”). Compare Galician chorar and Spanish llorar.

more.definition: nose (a protuberance on the face housing the nostrils, which are used to breathe or smell)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese nariz, from Late Latin nārīcem f, ultimately derived from Latin nāris. Compare Galician nariz m, Asturian, Aragonese, Ladino, and Spanish nariz f, Italian narice f.

more.definition: even
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese par, from Latin pār (“equal, like”).

more.definition: pair; partner; couple
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese par, from Latin pār (“equal, like”).

more.definition: quiet (with little or no sound); quiet (having little motion or activity; calm); quiet (not talking much or not talking loudly; reserved)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin quiētus. Doublet of quedo and quite, which were inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese.

more.definition: to decide; to determine; to resolve
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēcīdere, with change of conjugation.

more.definition: down, downwards (towards a lower place)
more.etymology: Egyptian 𓃾 (kꜣ)der. Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ)bor. Ancient Greek Α (A)bor. Etruscan 𐌀 (a)influ. From a (“at”) + baixo (“low”).

more.definition: ancient (related to ancient times); old (less often of people); former
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese antigo, from Latin antīquus (variant antīcus).

more.definition: pass (document granting admission or permission to pass); pass (the act of moving the ball to another player); an employment contract
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-der. Latin -ereinflu. English passsl. Portuguese passardeverb. Deverbal from passar (“to pass”).

more.definition: girl, young lady
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese moça.

more.definition: dark
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese escuro, scuro, oscuro, from Latin obscūrus. Doublet of obscuro. Compare Sicilian scuru.

more.definition: band, stripe; side; bend
more.etymology: Borrowed from French bande (“ribbon”), from Frankish *bindā (“join, link”).

more.definition: value (numerical quantity measured, assigned or computed); value (the degree of importance one gives to something); price; cost
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese valor, from Late Latin valōrem.

more.definition: clock (instrument to measure or keep track of time); watch
more.etymology: Borrowed from Spanish reloj, from Old Catalan relotge, from the older orollotge, from Latin hōrologium (“sundial”), from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). Doublet of horológio, a borrowing. Compare Galician reloxo, Mirandese reloijo, Asturian and Leonese reló, Spanish reloj, Aragonese reloch, Catalan rellotge and Occitan relòtge.

more.definition: species; type, sort, kind; a document classification according to its disposition or nature
more.etymology: Latin speciēslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin speciēs. Compare Spanish especie, French espèce.

more.definition: guilty
pleasant, agreeable, nice
more.etymology: From agradar (“to please”) + -ável. Compare Catalan and Spanish agradable, French agréable and Italian (ag)gradevole.

senses.gloss_en: to get, to obtain, to procure, to provide with

more.definition: to fix; to set up; to set
more.etymology: Derived from Old French arrumer. Compare with arrimar. Perhaps from Proto-Celtic *ad-φrima-Ø.

more.definition: majesty (the quality of being impressive and great)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese magestade, majestade, borrowed from Latin maiestātem.

more.definition: to break (end up or cause to end up in two or more pieces that cannot easily be reassembled); to fracture a bone; to break down (stop, or to cause to stop, functioning properly or altogether)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese quebrar, itself, through metathesis, from Latin crepāre (“to crack, to creak”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂-.

fr: fr:mettre la clé sous la porte:verb

more.definition: to desist; to give up; to revoke
more.etymology: Latin dēsisterelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin dēsistere.

more.definition: million (10⁶); a type corn with a tall and large kernels
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Italian milionebor. Borrowed from Italian milione.

more.definition: to hurt (to cause physical pain); to hurt (to cause emotional pain)
more.etymology: From the verb machar (“to grind”), from macho (“mallet”), from Latin marculus (“small hammer”). Compare Spanish machucar.

more.definition: should (indicates that an action is considered by the speaker to be obligatory); ought (indicates that the subject of the sentence has some obligation to execute the sentence predicate.); will likely (indicates that the subject of the sentence is likely to execute the sentence predicate.)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dever, from Latin dēbēre (“to owe, to must”).

more.definition: over, finished (that no longer continues); finished, polished (improved beyond what is necessary); exhausted, depleted, used up (whose resources have been consumed entirely)
more.etymology: Past participle of acabar.

more.definition: hence; therefore
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *próder. Proto-Indo-European *sóder. Proto-Indo-European *-tosder. From por (“for”) + tanto (“so much”). Compare Spanish por lo tanto, as well as related constructions with Italian pertanto and French partant.

more.definition: survive; outlive; keep going, keep on
more.etymology: From Latin supervīvere (“to survive, to outlive”).

more.definition: to close; to conclude (an agreement); to complete (all levels of a video game)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fechar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Vulgar Latin pesclum, from Latin pessulus (“bolt”). Probably a southern Portuguese variant, with the change of /p/ to /f/ reflecting Arabic influence. By surface analysis, fecho + -ar.

more.definition: princess; princess, a beautiful woman; a young girl; used as a term of endearment
more.etymology: French princessebor. Borrowed from French princesse.

more.definition: normally
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ǵn̥h₃sḱétider. Ancient Greek γνώμων (gnṓmōn)bor. Latin normālislbor. From normal + -mente.

more.definition: stopped, halted, immobile; standing
more.etymology: Past participle of parar.

more.definition: hearing; ear, especially the inner part of the ear
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese ouvydo (displacing collateral form oydo), from earlier *ouido, from Latin audītus.

more.definition: to replace, to substitute (to remove something and put a new one in its place); to change (to dispose of something one owns or is using and get a new one); to trade; to exchange
more.etymology: First used in the 14th century, from Old Galician-Portuguese trocar, from Medieval Latin trocāre; further etymology uncertain (probably Frankish *trokōn). Cognate with Spanish, Galician, Catalan, and Occitan trocar, French troquer, English truck.

more.definition: correct; corrected, amended
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin correctus (“improved, amended, correct”), past participle of corrigere, conrigere (“to make straight, make right, make better, improve, correct”), from com- (“together”) + regere (“to make straight, rule”). Cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese correyto, which may have been inherited.

more.definition: relationship (connection or association); the act of relating (making a connection); relationship (a romantic or sexual involvement)
more.etymology: From relacionar (“to relate; to make a connection”) + -mento, from relação (“relation”), from Latin relātiō (“bringing back”).

senses.gloss_en: to get, to obtain, to procure, to provide with

more.definition: to obtain, get
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin obtinēre, with conjugation based on ter.

more.definition: pants (garment covering the body from the waist downwards)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese calças, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

more.definition: bottle
more.etymology: Arabic غَرَّافَة (ḡarrāfa)bor. Borrowed from Arabic غَرَّافَة (ḡarrāfa).

more.definition: to lie (to affirm as true what is known to be false, or to deny what is known to be true); to deceive, to lie; to fail
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mentir, from Latin mentīrī.

more.definition: apparently; seemingly
more.etymology: From aparente + -mente.

more.definition: society (group of people sharing culture); society (group of persons who meet to engage in a common interest); society (people of one’s country or community taken as a whole)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin societātem (“society, community”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, companion, ally”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-yo- (“companion”), from *sekʷ- (“to follow”).

more.definition: to fly
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese voar, from Latin volāre (“to fly”). Compare Galician voar and Spanish volar.

more.definition: to do something; to act; to function; to perform; to conduct oneself in a specific manner; to behave; to proceed
more.etymology: French agirbor. Borrowed from French agir, from Latin agere.

more.definition: to send; to bring forth
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese enviar, from Late Latin inviāre, from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Spanish and Catalan enviar, French envoyer, Italian inviare.

more.definition: black; black in colour; being the darkest of its kind; black (dark-skinned)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese preto (“black, near”), from earlier *apreto, from apretar (Modern Portuguese apertar (“tighten, press, clamp”)), from Late Latin appectorāre, from Latin pectus (“chest”). The semantic evolution to "black" or "dark" comes through the sense of "dense" or "thick". Another common, but less likely, etymology suggested is a Vulgar Latin *prettus, from pressus. Doublet of perto.

more.definition: connected, linked; turned on, activated; bandaged
more.etymology: From ligar + -ado.

more.definition: ghost (spirit appearing after death)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin phantasma (“apparition, specter”), from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “an appearance, image, apparition, specter”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to make visible”). Doublet of abantesma.

more.definition: height; altitude; moment, period (in time, usually referring to the past)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese altura, from alto + -ura.

more.definition: crazy, mad
more.etymology: Unknown. Maybe from maluco (“moluccan”)- see Moluccas - or from a diminutive of malo.

senses.gloss_en: to live, to lodge, to reside, to dwell

more.definition: to live, reside (have permanent residence)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese morar, possibly a learned borrowing from Latin morārī.

more.definition: colleague (fellow member of a profession or staff); mate (a comrade or fellow with whom an activity or place is shared); classmate
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Latin collēgalbor. Learned borrowing from Latin collēga (“a partner in office”).

more.definition: pig (the domesticated farm animal Sus scrofa); pork; swineflesh; pig (dirty or slovenly person)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). Compare Galician porco.

more.definition: personally; in person
more.etymology: From pessoal + -mente.

more.definition: natural; native of, from; room-temperature (of liquids)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese natural, borrowed from Latin nātūrālis.

more.definition: after a long time; eventually; at last; anyways; whatever
more.etymology: From em (“in”) + fim (“the end”). From Latin in fine. Compare French enfin.

more.definition: to visit
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese visitar, from Latin vīsitāre (“to see, to visit”).

more.definition: the act or result of diverging (to tend into different directions); diversion (tactic used to draw attention away from the real threat or action); the act of entertaining
more.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dīversiōnem, from Latin dīversus (“opposite; apart; diverse”), past participle of dīvertō (“to divert; to separate”).

more.definition: firm
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese firme, from Vulgar Latin firmis, from Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).

senses.gloss_en: to fit, to suit, to go with

more.definition: to serve (to work as a servant for someone); to serve (to worship a god); to serve (to give out or place down food or drink)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese servir, from Latin servīre.

more.definition: couple, married couple; pair; a pair consisting of a male and a female
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese casal, from Late Latin casālis (“domestic, belonging to the house”) or casāle (“country house, farm”), ultimately from casa. Compare Italian casale, Old French chesal, Spanish casal.

more.definition: open
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₂epóder. Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer-der. Proto-Indo-European *-yetider. Latin aperiōder. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aberto, from Latin apertus.

more.definition: song
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cançon, from Latin cantiōnem. Doublet of chanson.

more.definition: woods, forest (collection of trees); dodgeball
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese mata, possibly from Late Latin matta (“reed mat”).

more.definition: thanks (expression of gratitude or satisfaction)
digit, a part of the body inclusive of fingers or toes; finger, the width of a finger as an approximate unit of length; dedo, a traditional Portuguese unit of measurement about equal to 1.8 cm
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dedo, from Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”). Doublet of dígito, which was borrowed. Compare Galician dedo, Spanish dedo, and Catalan dit.

more.definition: tape, ribbon, band; film, movie; cartridge
more.etymology: Uncertain. Likely from Latin vitta (“band, ribbon”).

more.definition: honest (scrupulous with regard to telling the truth)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese onesto, from Latin honestus, from honor.

more.definition: objective; aim; goal
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin objectīvus.

senses.gloss_en: to construct, to erect, to build

more.definition: to build; to construct
more.etymology: Latin cōnstruerelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin cōnstruere.

more.definition: sensation, sense
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sent-der. Medieval Latin sēnsātiōnemlbor. Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sēnsātiōnem, from Latin sēnsus + -ātiō.

more.definition: proud
more.etymology: From orgulho (“pride”) + -oso.

more.definition: to laugh (to express mirth or derision by emitting chuckling sounds); to laugh at; to make fun of (to make an object of ridicule); to laugh (to be or appear mirthful)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese riir, from Vulgar Latin *rīdīre, from Latin rīdēre.

more.definition: throw (act of throwing something); bid (offer at an auction); a series of actions carried out during a game
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Portuguese lançardeverb. Deverbal from lançar.

more.definition: to attack (to apply violent force); to attack (to aggressively challenge a person or idea); to attack (to deal with something in a direct way)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Middle French destacherbor. Italian attaccarebor. Borrowed from Italian attaccare (“to join; to attack”).

more.definition: happiness (state of someone who is happy); happy event; good luck; good fortune; luck; ventura
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīcitātem. Cognate with Galician felicidade.

more.definition: mountain
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese montanna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

more.definition: mood (mental state); humour; bodily fluid; humour (one of the four basic bodily fluids in humourism)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese umor, humor, a borrowing from Latin hūmōrem (“humour, fluid”).

more.definition: Brazilian Portuguese standard spelling of prémio
exact; accurate; precise
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exāctus.

more.definition: homicide (killing of a person by another); manslaughter (the non-premeditated and/or justifiable killing of another person by another person)
more.etymology: Latin -iusnom. Latin homicīdiumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin homicīdium.

senses.gloss_en: to balk, to block, to hinder stop, to delay

more.definition: to prevent; to impede, stop; to hinder, block
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin impedīre. Cf. the related empecer.

more.definition: glass (vessel from which one drinks)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *kewp-der. Inherited from Late Latin *cuppu, from cūppa, from Latin cūpa, possibly influenced by Frankish *kopp.

more.definition: full, complete; completed
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin complētus.

more.definition: false; untrue; not factual; wrong; false; artificial; fake; false
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese falso, from Latin falsus (“deceived”), from fallō (“to deceive”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰwel- (“to lie, deceive”).

more.definition: cape (piece of land extending beyond the coast); the final steps or moments of an event; corporal (rank below a sergeant)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cabo (“besides; nearby”), from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-. Doublet of caput, chefe, and chef.

more.definition: to grow (become bigger or taller); to grow up (to become older); to grow in number or extent
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese crecer, from Latin crēscere (“to grow”), from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).

more.definition: via (by way of; passing through); via (by means of; using a medium)
more.etymology: Latin viālbor. Learned borrowing from Latin viā (“by way of”).

more.definition: prepared, ready; qualified, well-qualified
more.etymology: Derived from Latin praeparātus (“prepared, having been prepared”).
Proto-Semitic *manpayder. Proto-Semitic *manpiy-der. Latin mappalbor. Italian mappa fbor. Borrowed from Italian mappa f (“map”), a learned borrowing from Latin mappa (“napkin”), of Punic origin.

senses.gloss_en: to find out, to discover, to figure out, to learn

more.definition: to understand; to realize, to notice; to perceive
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *per-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perceber, from Latin percipere.

more.definition: blow (act of striking or hitting); blow (unfortunate occurrence); a decisive act or occurrence
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese colbe, golbe, from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus (“blow; cuff”), from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos, “blow; slap”). Some sources believe it to have been introduced through a Gallo-Romance intermediate such as Old Occitan colp, although this is uncertain. It may alternatively be a derivative of an Old Portuguese verb golpar, golbar. Compare Spanish golpe.

more.definition: talk; lecture; speech (session of speaking); discourse (expression in (spoken or written) words)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Latin discursuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin discursus.

more.definition: obvious
more.etymology: Latin obviuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin obvius.

more.definition: attempt, trial, experiment
more.etymology: Nominalization of the feminine singular of tentativo.

more.definition: frightening; scary; frightful
more.etymology: From assustar + -dor.

more.definition: to hold; to grasp; to make safe; to hold back (act with reserve; contain one’s full measure or power)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese segurar, from seguro (“safe”), from Latin sēcūrus (“careless; unconcerned”).

more.definition: intention, intent
more.etymology: Modified (to more closely reflect the Latin word) from Old Galician-Portuguese entençon, from Latin intentiōnem (or borrowed directly from it later).

senses.gloss_en: to cry out, to shriek, to scream, to yell

more.definition: to shout, to scream, to yell
more.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.

more.definition: evidence
more.etymology: Latin ēvidentialbor. Learned borrowing from Latin ēvidentia.

more.definition: a flat dish from which food is served or eaten; a course at a meal; cymbal
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prato, a semi-learned borrowing from Vulgar Latin *plattus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide; broad”), from Proto-Hellenic *plətús, from Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us, from *pleth₂- + *-us. Doublet of the popularly inherited chato and the Hellenism plati-.

more.definition: foolish; silly (having or characterised by poor judgement or little intelligence); a whiny kid
more.etymology: Unknown. Maybe from Latin stolidus (“foolish”) or tōles (“tonsilitis”).

more.definition: to breathe
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin respīrāre.

more.definition: closed, shut; locked
more.etymology: Past participle of fechar (“to close”).

more.definition: act (deed); act (state of existence); act (process of doing something)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctus, from agere. Doublet of auto.

more.definition: to study
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estudar, from estudo + -ar, from Latin studium. Compare Latin studēre. Compare Spanish estudiar.

more.definition: joy, happiness; party; fun; synonym of gergelim
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alegria. By surface analysis, alegre (“happy”) + -ia.

more.definition: to wear; to don (to have an item of clothing on oneself); to put on (to put an item of clothing on oneself); to get dressed (to put clothes on oneself)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-yétider. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vestir, from Latin vestiō.

senses.gloss_en: to imprison, to put into confinement after judicial writ (the state of which is called Haft) (this is the most common signification in its strict definition, of which however legal laymen may deviate to mean any kind of government arrest)

more.definition: to arrest (to seize and take into legal custody); to attach or bind; to restrain; to restrict
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese prender, from Latin prēndere, variant of prehendere (“to seize; to detain”), from prae- (“before”) + *hendō (“to take, to seize”) (not attested without prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

more.definition: to move, to mess with, to put your hands on; to fiddle with; to move it; to hurry up
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mecer, from Latin miscēre (“to mix”). Compare Spanish mecer.

more.definition: to treat (to handle, deal with or behave towards in a specific way); to deal with, to handle, to take care of; to treat (to apply medical care to a person)
more.etymology: Semi-learned form modified from older tractar, borrowed from Latin tractāre (“to drag; to handle; to practice”), from tractus (“dragged”), perfect passive participle of trahō (“to drag; to extract”).

more.definition: recently
more.etymology: From recente + -mente.

more.definition: fire (occurrence of fire in a certain place); arson (criminal fire)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(s)kend-der. Latin -iusnom. Latin incendiumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin incendium (“conflagration; fire”).

more.definition: sleep; sleepiness
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sono, from Latin somnum, from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos, from *swep- + *-nós. Compare Galician sono, Spanish sueño, Italian sonno and French sommeil.

more.definition: instant; moment (very brief period of time); instant (single point in time)
more.etymology: Latin īnstantemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin īnstantem (“urging; urgent”).

more.definition: a fall; drop; crash
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese caeda, from Vulgar Latin *cadeta (“a falling, drop”) feminine past participle of *cadescere, from Latin cadere. Compare Spanish caída.

more.definition: pocket; one's finances or acquisitive power
more.etymology: Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa)der. From bolsa + -o (forms the masculine).

more.definition: in separate pieces; fragmented; broken; not working properly; broken; having the bone in pieces; fractured; broken
more.etymology: From quebrar + -ado.

more.definition: similar
secret
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *s(w)éder. Proto-Indo-European *krey-der. Latin sēcrētuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin sēcrētus. Doublet of segredo.

more.definition: to permit, to allow, to let; to permit (to give occasion to); to tolerate
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin permittere, with change of conjugation.

more.definition: guest
soil, ground; solo (a piece of music for one performer)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin solum (“soil, ground”).

more.definition: to forgive; to justify; to apologise (to make an apology or excuse)
rest, day off (from work); respite; break (a brief interval of rest or relief); slack (extent to which a part of a mechanism can move freely)
more.etymology: Deverbal from folgar. Compare Spanish huelga (“strike”).

more.definition: rule (a regulation, law or guideline)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēgula as a semi-learned term. Compare Spanish regla. Cf. the inherited doublet relha, reixa and also the borrowed régua.

more.definition: confusing (difficult to understand); confused (unable to think clearly, disoriented); confused; muddled (disorganized, in disarray)
more.etymology: Latin cōnfūsuslbor. Learned borrowing from Latin cōnfūsus (“mixed, mingled”), from cōnfundō (literally “to pour together”).

more.definition: to move (change position); to induce; to persuade; to sue (file legal action)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mover, from Latin movēre. Compare Spanish mover, French mouvoir.

more.definition: miracle (wonderful event attributed to supernatural powers); miracle (fortunate outcome that prevails despite overwhelming odds against it)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese miragre, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”). Compare Spanish milagro. Doublet of miráculo, a more recent borrowing.

more.definition: heavy (having great weight); heavy, deep, intense (of great force or intensity)
more.etymology: Past participle of pesar. From Old Galician-Portuguese pesado.

more.definition: connection
more.etymology: From Latin connexiōnem (“a conclusion, binding together”), from connectō, an alternative spelling of cōnectō (“to bind together”), from compound of co- (“together”) and nectō (“to bind”).

more.definition: tale, story (account of an asserted fact or circumstance); short story (work of fiction shorter than a novel); five euros
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese conto, from Vulgar Latin *contu(s), *comptu(s), from Latin computus (“calculation”). Doublet of cômputo.

more.definition: to kiss
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese beijar, from Latin bāsiāre.

more.definition: feeling, emotion, sentiment
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *sent-der. Latin sentimentumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin sentimentum.

more.definition: to listen to; to hear (to perceive sound)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-der. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escuitar, ascuitar, ascoitar, from Latin ascultāre. Compare Galician escoitar. Doublet of auscultar, a borrowing from Latin.

more.definition: passerine (any bird of the order Passeriformes)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese passaro, from Vulgar Latin *passarum, from Latin passer (“sparrow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *p(e)t-tro- (“who flies, bird”), from *peth₂- (“to fly”). Compare English passerine, Spanish pájaro, Dalmatian paserain, Romanian pasăre.

more.definition: upper, higher; better; superior
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin superiōrem.

more.definition: calm; serene
more.etymology: From calma.

senses.gloss_en: to take, to take over, to assume

more.definition: to assume (to take on a position or duty); to take responsibility (to blame oneself for something; to acknowledge a fault); to take responsibility (to accept an obligation or liability)
more.etymology: Latin assūmerelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin assūmere.

more.definition: fear, awe; concern, apprehension, trepidation
more.etymology: Deverbal from recear.

more.definition: period (geochronologic unit of millions years); a school year interval (in pre-university education) of approximately three months; period (menstruation)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin periodus, a learned borrowing from Ancient Greek περῐ́οδος (perĭ́odos, “going round in a circle, periodic recurrence”).

more.definition: throat (posterior region of the oral cavity); throat (anterior-superior part of the neck); canyon, narrow (narrow passage between mountains)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese garganta; from a substrate language *gʷr̥h₃gn̥t- (“throat”), cognate with Proto-Celtic *brāgants (“neck, throat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”). Alternatively, onomatopoeic.

more.definition: task, job; burden, chore; piece work (type of employment where wages are calculated per unit of tasks performed)
more.etymology: From Arabic طَرِيحَة (ṭarīḥa, “endeavor”), a semantic narrowing of طَرِيحَة (ṭarīḥa, “something thrown down”), a (now unproductive) patient noun form of طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw”). Cognate with Galician tarefa and Spanish tarea.

more.definition: lady; queen; king (a piece of checkers that reached the farthest row forward)
more.etymology: Borrowed from French dame, from Latin domina. Doublet of dona.

more.definition: painting; picture; square; rigid, generally rectangular mounting for a painting
more.etymology: From Latin quadrum. Compare Galician cadro, Spanish cuadro, and Italian quadro.

more.definition: vote (a formalised choice); vote (act or instance of participating in such a choice); vow (solemn promise to perform some act, or behave in a specified manner)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese voto, partly borrowed from Latin vōtum (“vow”), itself from voveō (“to vow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ-. Doublet of the inherited bodo (“food, money, or clothes given to the poor on holy days”) and boda (“wedding”).

more.definition: to cook (food), to bake; to fire (heat (pottery, etc.))
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cozinnar, from Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. Compare Galician cociñar, Spanish cocinar.

more.definition: to divide, separate; to share; to divide
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁-der. Latin dīviderelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin dīvidere (“to divide, separate”).

more.definition: town; country house; a low-class residential area, like row houses, but in a self-managed community around a cul-de-sac
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese vila (“village”), from Latin villa (“country house”). Cognate with Galician vila, Spanish and Italian villa, and French ville. The sense of a slum is a semantic loan from Spanish villa.

more.definition: possibility
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin possibilitātem.

more.definition: easily
more.etymology: From fácil + -mente.

more.definition: treasure (collection of valuable things); Treasury (department responsible for management of public revenue); treasure (any single thing that one values greatly)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tesouro, from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure; hoard”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse; treasure”). Doublet of the borrowing tesauro.

more.definition: a thought; an idea; thinking (process by which thoughts arise); ideology (beliefs and principle of a group)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese penssamento, from penssar (“to think”) + -mento, from Latin pēnsāre (“to ponder”).

senses.gloss_en: to hurt, to damage, to harm

more.definition: to spoil, to damage, to corrupt, to ruin, to break; to botch, bungle; to go bad (of foods and commodities)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese estragar, from Vulgar Latin *strāgāre, from Latin strāgēs (“defeat, slaughter”).

senses.gloss_en: to convince, to persuade, to satisfy

more.definition: to convince (make someone believe, or feel sure about something)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese convencer, from Latin convincere.

more.definition: to hit (a target); to get something right; to adjust
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese acertar. By surface analysis, a- + certo + -ar. Compare Galician and Spanish acertar and English ascertain.

more.definition: glass (the material)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vidro, from Latin vitreus, from vitrum, from Proto-Indo-European *wed-ro- (“water-like”), from *wed- (“water”). Cognate with Galician vidro, Spanish vidrio.

more.definition: illegal; unlawful (forbidden by the law)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin illēgālis, from Latin lēgālis. By surface analysis, i- + legal.

examples.text: Eu vou para a escola de bicicleta.

translations.de: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule.
translations.en: I ride my bicycle to school.
translations.fr: Je vais à l'école à vélo.

examples.text: As bicicletas estão na garagem.

translations.de: Die Fahrräder stehen in der Garage.
translations.en: The bicycles are in the garage.
translations.fr: Les vélos sont dans le garage.

more.definition: bicycle (vehicle); bicycle kick (a kick in which the kicker leans backwards and kicks the ball back over his head)
collocations: andar de bicicleta — to ride a bike
more.etymology: Borrowed from French bicyclette, from Latin bi- (“two”) + Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle, wheel”). By surface analysis, biciclo + -eta.

more.definition: tail; butt, buttocks
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rabo, from Latin rāpum.

more.definition: departure (act of departing); start (beginning point of a race); match (sporting event)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese partida, from partir (“to depart”), from Latin partīre (“to part”), from pars (“part”).

more.definition: champion
more.etymology: Borrowed from Italian campione (cf. also French champion), from Medieval Latin or Late Latin campiōnem (“champion, fighter”), from Frankish *kampijō (or a Lombardic equivalent) from Proto-Germanic *kampijô, based on Latin campus (“level ground”).

more.definition: chamber; council; ellipsis of câmara municipal
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese camara, from Vulgar Latin camara, from Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára).

more.definition: name, reputation
mystery (something that is unexplained)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mystērium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion, “a mystery, a secret, a secret rite”), from μύστης (mústēs, “initiated one”), from μυέω (muéō, “to initiate”), from μύω (múō, “to shut”).

more.definition: quantity, amount
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin quantitātem.

senses.gloss_en: to jump, to leap, to spring

more.definition: to jump, to propel oneself upward; to jump over, to propel oneself over; to skip, to omit, to disregard
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin pullāre.

more.definition: paradise; heaven
more.etymology: Proto-Iranian *paridayjahder. Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos)bor. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese parayso, from Latin paradīsus, borrowed from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.

more.definition: to disappear; to vanish (to become lost, unseen or stop existing); to make something disappear; to get rid of
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *trísinflu. From des- + aparecer (“to appear”).

more.definition: a battle, especially a short one; skirmish; fighting, or a fight, in a sport context; fierce campaigning or effort against something; war
a painting; painting
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese pintura, from Vulgar Latin *pinctūra, from Latin pictūra.

more.definition: concern, worry (act or effect of worrying or being concerned); care; restlessness
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Latin praeoccupātiōnemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin praeoccupātiōnem. By surface analysis, preocupar + -ção.

more.definition: to calm; to calm down (to make calm); to calm down (to become calm); to calm down (to become less agitated)
more.etymology: Latin -ereinflu. From a- + calmo (“calm”) + -ar.

more.definition: short (having a small distance between ends or edges); short (of little duration)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese curto, corto, from Latin curtus, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-, *(s)k(ʷ)Art-, *(s)k(ʷ)Ard- (“short”).

more.definition: proprietress; female owner; female housekeeper; governess; housewife; married woman; wife
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese dona, from Late Latin domna, from Latin domina. Doublet of dama. Compare Spanish doña, dueña.

more.definition: to take, appropriate; to avail, to seize; utilize, to use; to be useful
more.etymology: From a- + proveito + -ar.

more.definition: building, edifice
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-der. Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Latin -iusnom. Latin aedificiumlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin aedificium.

more.definition: to carry; to load (put wares into a vehicle); to load (load a software into the primary memory)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese carregar, from Late Latin carricāre (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“a car, wagon”), from Gaulish.

more.definition: to increase (become larger); to increase, augment (cause something to become larger)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin augmentāre, from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”). Cognate of English augment.

more.definition: to endure hardship physically and/or emotionally; to undergo, to experience, especially in a negative way
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sofrer, soffrer, from Vulgar Latin *sufferere or *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

senses.gloss_en: to forgive, to excuse, to pardon

more.definition: to forgive; to pardon; to pardon (to grant an official pardon for a crime); to treat mercifully
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *per-der. Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perdõar (“to forgive”), from Late Latin perdōnāre.

senses.gloss_en: to detach, to untie, to undo

more.definition: to release, to let go
more.etymology: From solto + -ar or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *soltāre (a root) < *solutāre, as a frequentative of Latin solvere.

more.definition: to share (to give); to share
more.etymology: From com- + partilhar.

more.definition: bro (a close friend); buddy; pal; mate (a friendly term of address for an unknown person); comrade (term of address used among communists)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *kh₂em-der. Proto-Indo-Iranian *kmáratider. Proto-Iranian *kamarāder. Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára)bor. Latin camerader. Spanish camaradabor. Borrowed from Spanish camarada.

more.definition: strange; weird (not normal); picky; particular (demanding to have things just right)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exquīsītus, perfect passive participle of exquīrō. Cognate with Spanish exquisito and English exquisite, both false friends.

more.definition: flower; a delicate, feminine woman or girl; surface
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese flor, a learned borrowing from Latin flos, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰléh₃s, from *bʰleh₃- + *-s. Compare Galician flor, chor.

more.definition: current; flow; electrical current; chain
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese corrente, from Latin currentem.

more.definition: calm; peaceful; tranquil (without motion or sound); calm, tranquil (free from emotional or mental disturbance)
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin tranquillus.

more.definition: to separate; to divorce (to dissolve a marriage)
more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin separāre. Cf. the inherited dialectal/archaic xebrar, still used in Galicia.

senses.gloss_en: to disturb, to interfere with, to hinder

more.definition: to bother; to annoy; to get annoyed; to bother (to feel care or concern)
more.etymology: Latin incommodārelbor. Learned borrowing from Latin incommodāre.

more.definition: to reach
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese alcançar, acalçar, from Old Spanish alcalçar, acalçar, from Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, from Latin calx (“chalk, finish line”).

more.definition: face; the cheek
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese façe, faz, from Latin faciēs. Doublet of fácies.

more.definition: crazy; out of one's mind
more.etymology: From earlier doudo, of uncertain origin. Possibly a doublet of dodô /dodó.

more.definition: pure (free of pollutants); pure; flawless (free of flaws or imperfections); pure; clean (free of immoral behaviour)

more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese valer, from Latin valēre, from Proto-Italic *walēō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥h₁éh₁yeti, from *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).

more.definition: egg (cell that results from the fertilization of the female gamete by the male gamete); egg (rounded body produced by oviparous females consisting of a membrane and outer shell that contains the embryo); this body, particularly that of chickens, when it has not yet been fertilized and is intended for food

more.definition: curious; inquisitive (tending to ask questions, investigate or explore); curious; odd; out of the ordinary
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys-der. Latin incūriōsusbf. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese curioso, from Latin cūriōsus.

more.definition: to experience; to experiment; to try (taste of food, fit of clothing etc.)

more.definition: bone; bone (material); a difficulty
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese osso, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os (“bone”), from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. more.definition: route (course or way travelled); combat (a fight or battle); defeat
more.etymology: Borrowed from Old French rote (modern French route).

senses.gloss_en: to think something over, to consider, to ponder, to contemplate

more.definition: to consider; to think highly of
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese considerar, from Latin cōnsīderāre.

more.definition: to walk (travel a distance by walking)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-mn̥der. Gaulish *kammanbor. Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, caminho (“path”) + -ar (forms 1st conjugation verbs).

more.definition: to last, endure

senses.gloss_en: to abandon, to leave, to quit, to forsake

more.definition: to abandon (to leave behind, especially something one was responsible for or associated with); to give up (to quit an activity or attempt); to let oneself be controlled by; to put oneself in the hands of; to indulge in
more.etymology: Proto-Germanic *bannanąder. Frankish *bannder. Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. French abandonnerbor. From French abandonner, from Old French abandoner, formed from a (“at, to”) + bandon (“jurisdiction, control”), from Late Latin bannum (“proclamation”), bannus, bandum, from Frankish *ban, *bann, from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to proclaim, command”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).

more.definition: left; left-hand; on or towards the left side
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esquerdo, from Old Spanish exquerdo, from Basque ezkerra, absolutive of ezker (“left hand; left side”), from Proto-Basque *ezkeR (“left hand”). more.definition: to hunt (chase down prey)
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese caçar, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus.

more.definition: meal (food that is prepared and eaten at a specific time)
more.etymology: Inherited from Latin refectiōnem.

more.definition: to put in; to insert into; to put (to place something somewhere); to meddle, interfere
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese meter, from Latin mittere (“to send, to put”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”).

more.definition: cadaver, corpse
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cadāver.

more.definition: trousers, pants; ring (on a mushroom)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese calça, from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

more.definition: shoe
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese çapato, çapata, from Old Spanish çapato, of unknown origin. Cognate with Galician zapato (“shoe”), Spanish zapato (“shoe”), Basque zapata (“shoe”), Catalan sabata (“shoe”), Occitan sabata (“shoe”), French savate (“worn-out (old) shoe”) and Italian ciabatta (“slipper”).

more.definition: paint; ink; dye
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese tinta, tĩta, from Latin tincta (“dyed”), perfect passive participle of tingō (“dye”, verb).

more.definition: to remain, stay, persist; to abide, reside
more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese permanescer, from a Vulgar Latin *permanēscere, an inchoative of Latin permanēre.

more.definition: to invite (ask for the presence or participation of someone)
more.etymology: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese convidar, from Vulgar Latin *convītāre, from Latin invītāre (“to invite”).

more.definition: show, spectacle

senses.gloss_en: to wish, to will, to want, to desire

more.definition: spongy, fluffy, soft; cute

more.definition: amiable, lovable, lovely; friendly, kind; courteous, engaging

more.definition: beast (any large animal); beast of burden (animal used to transport cargo); ass (any of several species of horse-like animals)

more.definition: reception (act of receiving); reception, front desk (the desk of a hotel, office etc. where guests are received)
more.etymology: Latin receptiōnemlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin receptiōnem (“the act of receiving; reception”).

senses.gloss_en: to breach, to break, to violate

more.etymology: Borrowed from Latin cancellāre (“to make like a lattice, to cover with a lattice, to cancel”), ultimately from cancer (“lattice, grid”), from Proto-Indo-European *geng- (“lump”). Doublet of chancelar, via French.

senses.gloss_en: to stop, to quit, to give up

more.definition: to drop, shed; to abandon, leave; to give up (stop or quit an activity etc.)
more.etymology: From largo + -ar.

more.definition: to celebrate, commemorate
more.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commemorāre.

more.definition: object; thing; that to which emotions or an action is directed towards; object (class or structure)

more.definition: to negotiate (buy, sell or exchange); to adjust, arrange; to expedite, facilitate (to favor the progress or completion of (subject, project) in order to obtain an agreement)
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-h₂tiinflu. Latin negōtiārīlbor. Learned borrowing from Latin negōtiārī.

more.definition: essay (written composition); an instance of practicing, rehearsal; a trial or test

more.etymology: From Old Galician-Portuguese sacrifiçio, sacrifiço, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin sacrificium (“sacrifice”), from sacrificō (“to sacrifice”), from sacer (“sacred”) + faciō (“do, make”). Displaced Old Portuguese sacrifiço.

more.definition: terrain (area of land or the particular features of it); land (real estate or landed property); field (wide, open space used to grow crops or to hold farm animals)

more.definition: conclusion; opinion (judicial opinion delivered by an Advocate General to the European Court of Justice for a legal solution in a case)

more.definition: dung; manure (of cattle); shit; bullshit, nonsense

more.definition: to thread (to put thread through an orifice, especially a pinhole); to stick (to place)
